title: The Empirical Effects of Unrelated Gameplay on Decision Quality in Digital Platforms
affiliations: University of New South Wales (UNSW), University of Queensland - Business School, Independent and

detail.title: The Empirical Effects of Unrelated Gameplay on Decision Quality in Digital Platforms

declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics Approval was received for this study

detail.abstract: The global gamification market is projected to exceed $180 billion by 2035, with major platforms, including Pinduoduo, Shopee, Alipay, and Home Shopping Network, embedding game-like features into shopping and payment contexts.This research examines whether unrelated gameplay embedded in digital platforms improves or impairs decision quality as consumers make repeated product choices. Three longitudinal experiments manipulate gameplay exposure across decision episodes, measuring decision accuracy, flow, and perceived skill over time. The dynamic state-space system models trajectories of individual decision accuracy across gameplay conditions. Results indicate that unrelated gameplay improves decision accuracy by accelerating learning dynamics rather than directly altering choices. Gameplay fosters flow and perceived skill that become integrated into the decision process, leading to more accurate decisions as experience accumulates. Flow reinforces perceived competence and influences subsequent performance, with effects persisting through learning dynamics. Game difficulty has little effect, but consumers' perceived competence and challenge during product choice determine whether gameplay improves decision accuracy. The findings help managers design digital platforms for both engagement and decision quality, while also assisting regulators assess whether platform designs benefit consumer welfare. Combining unrelated gameplay with choice decisions improves decision making when gameplay reinforces perceived competence without imposing attentional interference across tasks.

title: The Instagram Branding and the Psychological Mechanisms of Business Resilience
affiliations: and Independent Researcher

detail.title: The Instagram Branding and the Psychological Mechanisms of Business Resilience
detail.abstract: The rapid expansion of digital platforms has transformed branding practices, positioning Instagram as a strategic environment for the construction of entrepreneurial identity and business sustainability. This study examines how Instagram branding contributes to business resilience through underlying psychological mechanisms. Drawing on theories of self-presentation, social identity, emotional contagion, and perceived authenticity, the paper explores how consistent visual storytelling, value-driven communication, and audience interaction foster trust, loyalty, and adaptive capacity among small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). The analysis argues that resilience in the digital marketplace is not solely dependent on financial or operational flexibility, but also on psychologically embedded brand relationships that enhance customer commitment during periods of uncertainty. By synthesizing insights from branding research, digital entrepreneurship, and consumer psychology, the study proposes a conceptual framework linking Instagram-based branding strategies to cognitive and emotional processes that strengthen long-term business stability. The findings contribute to social media marketing literature by clarifying how platform-specific branding practices cultivate relational capital, reinforce brand meaning, and buffer firms against market disruptions. Practical implications highlight the importance of authenticity, narrative coherence, and community engagement in sustaining competitive advantage in digitally mediated environments.

title: From Pumps to Plugs: Value of Time and Charging Policies
affiliations: University of Rochester and University of Rochester - Simon Business School

detail.title: From Pumps to Plugs: Value of Time and Charging Policies
detail.abstract: Designing EV charging policies requires understanding how drivers trade off charging speed, price, and convenience. Using high-frequency vehicle telemetry data from Shanghai, we estimate a random-coefficient discrete-choice model of charging demand and provide field-based estimates of drivers' value of time (VOT) in charging. The mean VOT is 27% of the average wage, implying lifetime charging time costs of 1.7% of the vehicle price. Counterfactuals show that Level-III charging speed reduces driver time costs by 70% and explains 4.6% of new vehicle adoptions. We evaluate how improving vehicle charging speed, station power, and station density affect driver welfare.

title: Truncating the Tail: Wage Caps and the Human Capital Pipeline in Finance
affiliations: Independent, Shanghai University of Finance and Economics - College of Business,  and Shanghai Jiao Tong University (SJTU) - Antai College of Economics and Management

detail.title: Truncating the Tail: Wage Caps and the Human Capital Pipeline in Finance
detail.abstract: This paper examines how a unique Chinese policy that capped wages in the financial industry influenced the allocation of human capital. Leveraging the 2022 policy as a quasi-natural experiment, we use administrative university admissions data from 2017 to 2024 to analyze resulting shifts in students' major choices. We find that standardized admission scores for finance (economics) majors decreased by 0.071 (0.061) standard deviations, corresponding to a drop of 1.2 (1.0) percentiles within the provincial score distribution. This cooling effect is primarily driven by a contraction in student demand rather than adjustments in enrollment quotas. The observed decline is driven by both a reduction in expected pecuniary returns to financial sector jobs-amounting to as much as 20%-and the emergence of a "finance stigma" that lowered the perceived prestige of universities specialized in economics and finance. These effects are attenuated at elite universities and for new interdisciplinary majors such as internet finance. Overall, our results underscore the power of administrative interventions in reshaping the human capital pipeline.

detail.abstract: In January 2026, the Anthropic Economic Index reported a significant downward revision of global AI productivity projections from 1.8% to 1.0-1.2%, citing "hidden validation costs," error rates, and a necessary market retreat from full automation to augmentation. This empirical dataset, derived from over 1 million global conversations, presents a stark contrast to the speculative hype of the previous year but aligns precisely with the theoretical framework of Cognitive Divergence Theory (CDT) published 43 days earlier (Dec 3, 2025), representing a rare case of theoretical prediction preceding large-scale empirical measurement. This research note provides a comparative analysis between the empirical findings of Anthropic (January 2026) and the theoretical predictions of the Thermodynamics of Cognitive Power (Stan, Dec 3, 2025) and False Cognitive Power Transfer (Stan, Dec 31, 2025). We demonstrate that the "economic friction" identified by Anthropic is mathematically equivalent to "cognitive entropy", the energy loss mandated by the conservation of cognitive power when transferring tasks without underlying competence. The study concludes that the market's shift towards "Augmentation" validates the collapse of the "Level 1 Passenger" illusion, confirming the core tenets of Cognitive Divergence Theory: that AI acts as a competence multiplier, not a substitute for human cognitive energy.

title: Pricing Strategies for Incentivizing Influencer Information Sharing with Product Returns
affiliations: University of Texas at Austin - McCombs School of Business, New York University (NYU) - Department of Information, Operations, and Management Sciences and Shanghai University of Finance and Economics - College of Business

detail.title: Pricing Strategies for Incentivizing Influencer Information Sharing with Product Returns
detail.abstract: We examine how a firm can use pricing strategies to incentivize influencer information sharing in the presence of product returns. We develop a game theoretical model where the firm first sets the selling price, and the influencer subsequently decides whether to resolve customer valuation uncertainty via costly information sharing. The two parties adopt an imbalanced profit-sharing contract, under which they split profits from retained products, while the firm alone bears the delivery shipping cost for returned items. The firm maximizes its expected profit, whereas the influencer maximizes her utility, which weights both commission earnings and customer surplus. We find that when the unit shipping fee falls within a moderate range, the firm incentivizes influencer information sharing by setting either an upward- or downward-distorted informed price. The direction of price distortion depends on the magnitude of the unit shipping fee and on whether supply chain profit or customer surplus exerts a more dominant impact on the influencer's utility. We further show that return shipping coverage crowds out the influencer's role in resolving customer valuation uncertainty through information sharing, rendering the firm's pricing strategies ineffective. Additionally, we find that the firm strictly prefers a balanced profit-sharing contract to an imbalanced one; however, establishing such a balanced contract is subject to significant feasibility constraints.

title: Choice Design in Cause-related Marketing Campaigns for Societal Wellbeing: The Role of Regulatory Focus and Goal Framing
affiliations: Shanghai University, Shantou University - Business School, , Shanghai University and Shanghai University

detail.title: Choice Design in Cause-related Marketing Campaigns for Societal Wellbeing: The Role of Regulatory Focus and Goal Framing
detail.abstract: Choice design in cause-related marketing (CM) ads has valuable implications for maximizing marketing expenditures, particularly to explain when and why consumers respond more positively to a CM campaign. By conducting three laboratory experiments, this paper reveals the impact of choice design (with versus without choices) on consumers' responses to CM ads and the boundary conditions under which this impact occurs. Allowing consumers to decide who receives the donation leads to a higher sense of pride, resulting in a more positive attitude and stronger purchase intention after viewing the CM advertisement. This has important implications for both businesses and non-profit organizations, suggesting ways to improve advertising messages to support causes and societal well-being.

title: Bounded Misreporting Costs
affiliations: Purdue University - Daniels School of Business

detail.title: Bounded Misreporting Costs
detail.abstract: This study examines how limits on lying costs impact Sender/Receiver games. Individuals typically face limited penalties for nonviolent offenses that, in the context of a disclosure game, suggest bounds on the cost of lying. I examine a Sender/Receiver game where the Sender may be uninformed and/or may incur a cost of messaging. In the unique equilibrium, high types cannot fully separate if there is any finite bound on lying costs. The limited separation holds even if the type space is unbounded. Instead, high types collect into a single upper-tailed pool. If the limit on lying costs is sufficiently low, the only message distinguishes a single pool of high types from a single pool of low types. The composition of the high pool depends on the high types' ability to separate from low, otherwise nondisclosing types which, in turn, depends on the maximum lying costs. The results show that the maximum lying costs dictate whether any types can separate beyond a high-versus-low pool, and the amount of information potentially conveyed.

title: Towards Artificial General Intelligence: A Conceptual View on the Facilitating Role of Neurosymbolic Schemes
affiliations: University of Piraeus, University of Piraeus, Hellenic Open University, Hellenic Open University and Hellenic Open University

detail.title: Towards Artificial General Intelligence: A Conceptual View on the Facilitating Role of Neurosymbolic Schemes
detail.abstract: Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) is commonly associated with an agent's ability to operate across a wide range of tasks, environments, and problem domains, while maintaining robust performance under changing conditions. Despite recent advances in data-driven and learning-based approaches, existing artificial intelligence systems remain limited in their capacity to generalize beyond their training distributions and to preserve structural or normative constraints under distributional shift. neurosymbolic Artificial Intelligence has emerged as a promising paradigm for addressing these limitations by combining sub-symbolic learning with symbolic reasoning mechanisms. However, the theoretical role of neurosymbolic architectures in the context of AGI remains insufficiently formalized. In this paper, we investigate whether neurosymbolic AI can serve as a foundational paradigm for AGI from a learning-theoretic perspective. We introduce a formal framework based on task families with shared latent dynamics and varying observation models, and we define a minimal requirement for AGI-level generalization under constraint preservation. Building upon this framework, we provide an impossibility-style argument showing that, under observation non-identifiability and constraint-critical latent situations, purely end-to-end observation-to-action policies cannot, in general, satisfy uniform near-optimality and uniform constraint compliance across the entire environment family. We then interpret this obstruction as a structural implication: any architecture that achieves such uniform guarantees must effectively separate (i) environment-robust abstraction of observations from (ii) constraint-aware decision or verification in an environment-invariant space.

title: DynamiRAG: Dynamic Memory Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Entropy-Aware Hallucination Prediction
affiliations: Syracuse University and Syracuse University

detail.title: DynamiRAG: Dynamic Memory Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Entropy-Aware Hallucination Prediction
detail.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems remain susceptible to hallucination when retrieved evidence is noisy, contradictory, or insufficient. While recent adaptive RAG systems such as Self-RAG and SmartRAG address retrieval decisions, they lack mechanisms to assess retrieval quality prior to generation or to detect contradictions within retrieved evidence sets.This paper introduces DynamiRAG, a framework that augments standard RAG pipelines with four novel components: (1) a Retrieval Entropy Hallucination Predictor (REHP) that formalizes retrieval uncertainty via Shannon entropy to estimate hallucination risk before generation; (2) an Evidence Contradiction Detector (ECD) that identifies inter-document conflicts through semantic-lexical divergence analysis; (3) Multi-Hop Memory Chains (MHMC) that perform multi-step reasoning through residual vector arithmetic without requiring knowledge graphs; and (4) a Short-Term Memory cache (STM) enabling session-persistent retrieval acceleration. We evaluate DynamiRAG on HotpotQA under fair corpus-retrieval conditions. Our best configuration achieves 11.5% Exact Match and 16.8% F1, representing a +0.5% EM and +0.5% F1 improvement over the FiD baseline, with MHMCcontributing the largest individual gain (+2.0% EM over single-hop retrieval). We further report that Retrieval-Grounded Beam Scoring (RGBS), while theoretically motivated, decreases performance with small generators, providing insight into scale-dependent grounding effects. The ECD module successfully identifies contradictions in 97.5% of retrieval sets. Our analysis demonstrates that entropy-based retrieval quality signals, contradiction-aware evidence filtering, and memory-augmented multi-hop reasoning each address distinct failure modes in RAG systems.

title: The Private/public Law Divide in Digital Law

detail.title: The Private/public Law Divide in Digital Law
detail.abstract: As the digitization process of last decades affects the way of life, the need for digital law regulations is felt more. Thus, courts and scholars feel the need to categorize the digital law either under public law domain or under private law domain, so that the principles that govern the sub-discipline of digital law becomes clear. This study discusses the criteria that were employed since Romans for distinguishing public law from private law and analyses digital law, with its subcategories as to whether it falls under public law or private law. The study finds that public-private law divide is not perfectly severe, to classify every relation or dispute of law under one of the two domains and that digital law is not a field of law that can be categorized technically under either of these domains, but it can be related to the public sphere rather than the private sphere.

title: Why Enterprise Technology Investments Fail A Structural Cascade Model of Compounding Implementation Risk

detail.title: Why Enterprise Technology Investments Fail A Structural Cascade Model of Compounding Implementation Risk
detail.abstract: Enterprise technology investments fail at rates that have remained stubbornly consistent for decades, across industries, technology types, and organizational sizes. This paper argues that the reason is structural: organizations cannot close the gap between how they intend to adopt technology and how they actually do. The gap has nine identifiable conditions organized across four layers-Decision, People, Process, and Product-that compound from upstream to downstream through a cascade mechanism: Decision Layer failures increase the probability of People Layer failures, which amplify variance in Process Layer outcomes, which converge at Product Layer failure in ways that are traceable to upstream conditions, not to the product itself.

detail.abstract: Age assurance, parental control, and ultimately Youth safety systems for digital platforms fail systematically. This is not primarily due to technical limitations, but because parents, schools, and families actively circumvent them to meet practical needs. Drawing on research from multiple countries, this policy brief documents how up to two-thirds of underage social media accounts are created with parental assistance, device sharing renders device-level verification ineffective (particularly in lower-income households), and rigid app store age ratings force parents to falsify children's ages to access legitimate or desired services. The brief then examines emerging risks from AI chatbots, where an estimated 5.4 million U.S. youth have sought mental health advice despite minimal age verification or safety guardrails and where insufficient age and parental controls repeat patterns seen in social media's early expansion. Parental control tools show less than 1% adoption on major platforms because they are not fit-for-purpose, suffer from alert fatigue and false positives, operate in platform-specific silos, and rely on a surveillance model that research has linked to eroded family trust and no measurable protective effect. Structural incentives compound the problem: platforms earn over $11 billion annually from underage users, safety measures create competitive disadvantage, and age bans trigger migration to less-regulated alternatives with weaker safety infrastructure. The authors argue that effective policy must move beyond parental delegation and platform self-regulation toward safety-by-design standards, independent third-party risk assessment and safety standards, and regulatory frameworks that incentivize genuinely engaging, age-appropriate digital experiences rather than stripped-down versions of adult products

title: AI Hallucinations in Large Language Models: A Comprehensive Literature Review and the Imperative for Diverse AI Paradigms
affiliations: , California State University, Stanislaus - Department of Accounting & Finance and California State University, Stanislaus

detail.title: AI Hallucinations in Large Language Models: A Comprehensive Literature Review and the Imperative for Diverse AI Paradigms

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no conflicts of interest related to this research

detail.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable capabilities in natural language understanding and generation, yet they remain fundamentally limited by their propensity to produce hallucinations-outputs that are factually incorrect, logically inconsistent, or unsupported by their training data. The recent discovery by Shumailov et al. (2024) in Nature that AI models collapse when trained on recursively generated data has catalyzed urgent examination of LLM limitations and the broader trajectory of artificial intelligence development. This comprehensive literature review synthesizes recent research on AI hallucinations across multiple dimensions: definitions and taxonomies, fundamental mechanisms and root causes, detection and mitigation strategies, evaluation frameworks, and the critical phenomenon of model collapse from synthetic data contamination. We analyze 30 highly relevant studies published between 2023 and 2026, revealing that hallucinations stem from the probabilistic nature of autoregressive generation, training data limitations, architectural constraints, and fundamental gaps in semantic understanding. While numerous mitigation techniques have been proposed-including retrieval-augmented generation, chain-of-verification, and architectural innovations-no single solution eliminates hallucinations entirely. Critically, this review argues that LLMs represent just one architectural approach to artificial intelligence, and over-reliance on the LLM paradigm poses significant risks. We examine cascading effects of training models on AI-generated content, leading to irreversible model collapse. The review identifies urgent need for diverse AI paradigms-including symbolic AI, neuro-symbolic systems, and hybrid architectures-to create a robust, complementary ecosystem. Implications for information systems in accounting and auditing contexts are discussed, particularly regarding deployment of AI systems in high-stakes financial reporting and audit environments.

title: Subsidizing Crises: Evidence from Norway’s Electricity Market
affiliations: BI Norwegian Business School, Norwegian University of Life Sciences and HEC Montreal

detail.title: Subsidizing Crises: Evidence from Norway’s Electricity Market
detail.abstract: We examine consumer responses to the 2022 European Energy Crisis, using Norway’s zonal electricity market and the start of a subsidy policy as a natural experiment. Employing administrative consumption records from over 1.5 million households and a differences-in-differences approach, we show that zones more interconnected with Europe experienced a 7–9% reduction in household electricity consumption relative to zones less interconnected, with effects persisting for several months. Using a tripledifference approach, we find that heterogeneity in treatment effects is driven by household characteristics. Finally, exploiting the kink in the support schedule and using high-frequency data, we estimate local demand responsiveness at the point where the subsidy becomes binding. Overall, households reduced consumption, indicating that consumers adapted to the new high-price environment and viewed the subsidy as temporary, rather than responding in a conventional way to the immediate price relief.

title: Trade and Multinational Production Model
affiliations: ,  and World Bank

detail.title: Trade and Multinational Production Model
detail.abstract: This technical note introduces the Trade and Multinational Production (TMP) model as a tractable quantitative framework to jointly analyze trade and foreign direct investment in a multi-sector, input-output world. By embedding multinational production within a general equilibrium structure, the model captures firms' location decisions, input sourcing, and the propagation of shocks through global value chains. The TMP model provides a unified tool to simulate short- and long-run effects of trade and investment policy reforms, as well as the welfare implications of policy uncertainty.

title: Implications of Methodological Approaches in Decision Theory: A Conceptual Synthesis with Emphasis on Heuristics

detail.title: Implications of Methodological Approaches in Decision Theory: A Conceptual Synthesis with Emphasis on Heuristics

detail.abstract: Distinct theoretical frameworks have contributed to the development of Decision Theory, each offering specific insights into how decision-making occurs. This article aims to examine how methodological approaches across major frameworks in descriptive Decision Theory shape distinct perspectives on heuristics, intuition, and emotion, but with distinguished emphasis on heuristics. Methodologically, the study develops a conceptual synthesis that describes the core concepts of each framework and compares their methodological approaches and theoretical perspectives. The analysis begins with Bounded Rationality, as proposed by Herbert Simon, and then examines the Heuristics and Biases framework developed by Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky, Naturalistic Decision Making proposed by Gary Klein, Ecological Rationality associated with Gerd Gigerenzer, and Neuroeconomics advanced by Colin Camerer. The findings indicate that methodological approaches are not merely technical tools, but epistemic lenses that shape how cognitive mechanisms are identified, interpreted, and evaluated. Rather than reflecting purely theoretical disagreements, contrasting views on heuristics emerge from systematically different ways of observing and modeling decision processes. This article contributes to the literature by clarifying how methodological approaches shape theoretical perspectives in Decision Theory and by showing that different classes of heuristics (task-specific, general, and domain-specific) are associated with optimistic, skeptical, or more pragmatic views about the role and applicability of these mechanisms in decision-making.

title: Hidden Governance Failures in Nonprofits: Overlooked but Critical Issues of Communication, Records, and Authority

detail.title: Hidden Governance Failures in Nonprofits: Overlooked but Critical Issues of Communication, Records, and Authority

declarations.declarationOfInterest: n/a
declarations.funderStatement: n/a

detail.abstract: Nonprofit organizations, are widely studied in terms of formal governance structures, compliance, and fiduciary duties, yet many of the practical, everyday mechanisms that sustain organizational continuity remain overlooked. However, small charities and grant-dependent associations, often face governance challenges that are invisible yet highly consequential. While mainstream literature emphasizes board composition, fiduciary duties, and regulatory compliance, it largely ignores the procedural and infrastructural dimensions where governance actually operates. This book addresses that gap by examining the hidden mechanisms through which governance failures occur: communication practices, recordkeeping systems, and the exercise of authority within and across boards and staff. Drawing on organizational theory, archival science, and nonprofit practice, the book highlights how informal processes—such as the use of personal email accounts for official business, incomplete handovers, unclear signatory authority, and ambiguous roles of advisory boards—can create risks for accountability, continuity, and legal compliance. Through detailed analysis and practical guidance, this volume illuminates the invisible failures that threaten organizational legitimacy, disrupt succession, and impede mission continuity. By uncovering these overlooked but critical issues, the book provides nonprofit leaders, boards, and practitioners with a framework for strengthening governance infrastructure, preserving institutional memory, and mitigating risk before failures become visible crises.

title: Assessing Drivers of Psychosocial Stressors using Pythagorean Fuzzy Analytics in Ready-made Garments Industries of Emerging Economies
affiliations: Ahsanullah University of Science and Technology, Military Institute of Science and Technology, Ahsanullah University of Science and Technology, Ahsanullah University of Science and Technology, Ahsanullah University of Science and Technology and Ahsanullah University of Science and Technology

detail.title: Assessing Drivers of Psychosocial Stressors using Pythagorean Fuzzy Analytics in Ready-made Garments Industries of Emerging Economies
detail.abstract:
Bangladesh, an emerging economy, is among the world’s leading exporters of ready-made garments (RMG). Production costs are very low, and output is directed almost exclusively to Western markets. However, the industry’s precarious working conditions are recognized to have a substantial impact on workers’ social and psychological well-being. This study aimed to identify, prioritize, and examine the drivers of psychosocial stressors in the RMG industries of emerging economies, including Bangladesh. It applied Interval-Valued Pythagorean Fuzzy (IVPF) theory together with the Weighted Influence Non-linear Gauge System (WINGS) method. Following a comprehensive literature review and expert validation, 20 drivers were selected for analysis. The most critical were “Unpredictable scheduling and short notice changes” and “Perceived
organizational injustice and procedural opacity” with total engagement values of 0.11386 and 0.11127, respectively. Moreover, the causal ranking indicates that “Wage inadequacy and income instability” and “Abusive or unsupportive supervision” are the most influential drivers within the cause group. Their total position values are 0.00511 and 0.00394, respectively. Within the effect group, “Discrimination and occupational stigma” and “Ineffective grievance redress and unsafe
voice channels” register total position values of -0.00019 and -0.00059, respectively. The sensitivity analysis indicates only minor changes in total engagement and position values. It also shows that the rankings remain largely stable. These findings offer practical guidance for stakeholders and policymakers seeking to improve worker well-being and strengthen the
sustainability of the RMG industry in emerging economies.

title: Executive Decision-Making at the Intersection of Finance, Sales, and Logistics: A Unified Management Framework
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Executive Decision-Making at the Intersection of Finance, Sales, and Logistics: A Unified Management Framework
detail.abstract: Executive decision-making in contemporary organizations increasingly occurs at the intersection of multiple functional domains rather than within isolated managerial silos. Finance, sales, and logistics represent three of the most influential yet tightly interconnected decision areas in business management, particularly within mid-scale and growth-oriented firms. Decisions taken in one domain frequently generate immediate and often unintended consequences in the others, shaping profitability, cash flow stability, operational continuity, and strategic positioning. This article examines executive decision-making as an integrative managerial process that spans finance, sales, and logistics. It argues that traditional function-based decision models are insufficient for addressing the complexity and speed required of senior executives operating in volatile and competitive environments. Drawing on business management theory and executive-level practice, the study proposes a unified decision-making framework that aligns financial discipline, commercial objectives, and operational execution within a single managerial logic. The proposed framework emphasizes cross-functional visibility, integrated performance metrics, and shared accountability as key enablers of high-quality executive decisions. By reframing finance, sales, and logistics as interdependent decision domains, the article highlights how unified management structures can improve decision coherence, reduce risk exposure, and enhance organizational resilience. The study contributes to the business management literature by offering an original conceptual model that captures the realities of executive decision-making and provides practical insights for senior leaders seeking to navigate complex trade-offs and sustain long-term value creation.

detail.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is no more a vision of the future but an all-perceiving phenomenon that transforms all elements of society, not excluding education. Recently, the integration of AI technologies into education tools and platforms, as well as decision-making, has become an issue that is starting to gain significant impetus to the point where there is now a compelling need to impart AI literacy into the education of students, as well as to their teachers and administrators. At the same time, the capacity to comprehend, effectively critique, and communicate with AI developments has become a fundamental literacy among the learners of the 21st century. This paper discusses the multi-dimensional issues of the implications of AI literacy on education on three crucial aspects, including how AI literacy influences student learning, how AI literacy can be taught using pedagogical approaches, and the implications (ethical and societal implications) of integrating AI literacy into educational systems. To begin with, the paper explores the impact that the knowledge of AI concepts and tools has on cognitive engagement, critical thinking, digital adaptability, and better academic results among students. Second, the study looks at new and emerging pedagogical frameworks and curriculum design strategies that can support AI literacy, which includes project-based, interdisciplinary, and experiential learning using and with AI systems. Thirdly, it explores the ethical and societal consequences of AI literacy education; it focuses on such aspects as equity, algorithmic transparency, and responsible digital citizenship. The paper claims that AI literacy is not a technical field; it is a complete competence required to get through the world of AI out of awareness and agency. The educational systems can help ensure that more informed, inclusive, and empowered future citizens are created here by giving learners the ability to understand and critique AI systems. The study ends with a call to action to policymakers and educators to make AI literacy one of the foundational elements of the current education in the 21st century.

title: Project-Based Business Management in Furniture Design: Lessons from Custom Residential and Commercial Manufacturing
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Project-Based Business Management in Furniture Design: Lessons from Custom Residential and Commercial Manufacturing
detail.abstract: Furniture design and manufacturing has increasingly evolved into a project-based business environment, particularly within custom residential and commercial production contexts where each commission represents a distinct combination of design intent, client expectations, and operational constraints. Unlike standardized manufacturing systems, furniture design projects are characterized by high levels of customization, iterative decision-making, and close interaction between creative, managerial, and production functions. These characteristics challenge traditional functional and process-based management models, creating a need for business management approaches that are explicitly structured around projects rather than repetitive workflows. This article examines furniture design as a project-based business system, focusing on lessons derived from custom residential and commercial manufacturing environments. It argues that project-based business management is not merely an organizational choice in furniture design firms but a structural necessity driven by design variability, material specificity, and client involvement. The study conceptualizes furniture manufacturing projects as temporary yet strategically significant organizational units in which managerial decisions directly shape cost control, quality outcomes, timelines, and long-term client relationships.

title: The Economic Constitution: A Transdisciplinary Framework for Evaluating Policy Alignment Under Systemic Risk

detail.title: The Economic Constitution: A Transdisciplinary Framework for Evaluating Policy Alignment Under Systemic Risk

detail.abstract: This paper proposes a formal economic constitution grounded in two axiomatic principles: the maximization of human well-being and the maintenance of societal and ecological homeostasis. Unlike traditional economic policy models that rely on political discretion, ideological assumptions, or technocratic optimization, this framework evaluates all public policies using a universal logic filter based on declared goals, empirical impacts, and forecast viability. Drawing from constitutional economics, systems theory, and institutional design, it introduces mechanisms such as the Constitutional Well-Being Index (CWBI), the Civic Stability Index (CSI), and the Planetary Stability Indicator (PSI) to quantify alignment with constitutional aims. Policies that fail to meet threshold criteria for non-degradation or fall below forecast viability are subject to reversal, amendment, or suspension under oversight by a nonpartisan Economic Constitution Oversight Board (ECOB). The model redefines inflation, inequality, and fiscal sustainability not as standalone metrics but as system feedback signals, subordinate to well-being and stability. By embedding constitutional logic into economic governance, this framework offers a non-ideological, enforceable, and participatory foundation for aligning economic systems with democratic legitimacy, social justice, and long-term resilience.

title: One Prompt, One Paper: Should Academic Journals Expand Capacity with Generative AI?
affiliations: University of Florida - Department of Finance, Insurance and Real Estate and Aalto University, School of business

detail.title: One Prompt, One Paper: Should Academic Journals Expand Capacity with Generative AI?
detail.abstract: How should academic journals adapt as AI reshapes research? We develop a general equilibrium model where researchers use AI to accelerate production and a social planner sets capacity and submission fees. Without policy adjustment, submissions flood the system and acceptance rates collapse. With optimal fees, welfare rises monotonically with AI productivity regardless of whether referees also use AI. Fees decline as AI improves, even when review costs are fixed, because each dollar of fee screens more aggressively as production costs fall. Only 3% of the optimal fee internalizes direct review costs; the remaining 97% reflects congestion screening and prestige stabilization, a general equilibrium mechanism absent from standard Pigouvian analysis. Fee screening exceeds the review cost channel by more than an order of magnitude, and optimal capacity is near-flat across all scenarios.

title: Pricing AI as a Service
affiliations: New York University (NYU), Imperial College Business School and Imperial College Business School

detail.title: Pricing AI as a Service
detail.abstract: We study AI as a Service, in which a monopolistic provider sells downstream users access to AI agents/models. Motivated by prevalent contracting practices, we focus on conversation-based pricing (CBP), which charges a fixed fee per invocation, and outcome-based pricing (OBP), which charges only upon success. Buyers have private information about valuation and task difficulty, which determines the AI's success probability. We start with a binary-type model: CBP reduces to a standard screening problem, whereas OBP induces two-dimensional screening because success-contingent payments interact with type-dependent success probabilities. Under an OBP-specific increasing-differences condition, we characterise the optimal OBP menu and provide a "virtual type" interpretation that adjusts value by success probabilities. We show that OBP outperforms CBP when per-success value (value normalised by success probability) is aligned with success probability across segments; that is, buyers who are willing to pay more per success are also those for whom success occurs sufficiently often. When this alignment fails, CBP dominates. The underlying driver is a distinctive feature of OBP: a buyer may accept a high per-success price yet generate low, or even negative, expected profit for the provider. The same force yields an asymmetric robustness result: CBP guarantees at least half of second-best revenue, while OBP can be arbitrarily poor in the worst case. We apply the theory to a customer-service queueing setting in which a buyer deploys an AI service to handle incoming customer requests, and only unresolved requests are escalated to downstream human agents. We show that misalignment between AI capability and human service rate favours OBP, whereas aligned systems favour CBP. Finally, we extend the analysis to many types and show that the alignment logic continues to govern the comparison.

detail.abstract: This article discusses Herbert Simon's contributions to Behavioral Finance by comparing his ideas with the established literature in the field and reinterpreting them in the context of investment decisions, in order to clarify the intellectual genealogy of Behavioral Finance. In addition to revisiting the critique of homo economicus, it examines the concepts of bounded rationality, satisficing, intuition, and heuristics. Adopting a conceptual synthesis approach, the study organizes and integrates contributions from Simon's work and compares them with core Behavioral Finance literature. The comparison suggests that Simon's ideas are often compatible with those of prominent authors in Behavioral Finance and that several foundational themes of the field can be traced back to his work, supporting his positioning as a precursor to the field. It further illustrates how Simon's concepts apply meaningfully to investment decisions. The article highlights Simon's concept of intuition, which has received limited attention in Behavioral Finance. It also contributes to a clearer reconstruction of the intellectual genealogy of Behavioral Finance. By reinterpreting Simon's concepts primarily in light of Behavioral Finance research, the article contributes to debates about the evolution, epistemological foundations, and conceptual boundaries of the field.

detail.abstract:
As AI systems transition from generating content to executing real-world side effects—writing to databases, initiating transactions, modifying infrastructure—the governance problem shifts from monitoring outputs to authorizing actions. Monitoring architectures document what occurred; they do not determine whether an action was permitted before execution. This paper identifies a structural ambiguity emerging across regulatory consultations: the under-specification of the enforcement primitive at the boundary where AI intent becomes effect.

Distinguishing observability from authorization, the paper defines the architectural properties of an authorization boundary: non-bypassable gating, deterministic verdict semantics, fail-closed defaults, and policy-state binding. It argues that traditional compliance mechanisms—deterrence, accountability, escalation, and documentation—are structurally mismatched to autonomous systems operating at machine speed.

Drawing on cross-jurisdiction analysis, the paper proposes a Minimum Authorization Boundary Contract (MABC) for evidence-grade governance in agentic AI deployments. The argument is structural rather than empirical: the requirements follow from the engineering properties of autonomous systems and the regulatory trajectory of high-impact AI. Monitoring remains necessary, but enforcement must be layered beneath observability to produce architectures capable of both preventing unauthorized actions and documenting what occurred.

title: Generative Resilience: A Unified Theory of Sustained Competitive Advantage from Twenty-Five Years of Growth Through Disruption

detail.title: Generative Resilience: A Unified Theory of Sustained Competitive Advantage from Twenty-Five Years of Growth Through Disruption
detail.abstract: This paper synthesizes findings from a 25-year longitudinal research program (1999–2026) to propose a unified theory of Generative Resilience. Drawing on three interconnected studies—qualitative analysis of multi-horizon portfolios, empirical study of Fortune’s 100 Fastest Growing Companies, and quantitative analysis of counter-cyclical investment patterns—we argue that resilience is not a defensive posture designed to “bounce back” to a prior state. Rather, it is a generative capacity rooted in deliberate investment choices made within economic disruption that transform recessions into compounding competitive advantage. The theory is tested against the Tech Bust, the Great Recession, the COVID-19 pandemic, and the 2025–2026 “secondary shock” of trade policy volatility and AI transformation.

title: Augmentation Versus Substitution: Asymmetric Effects of Generative AI on Firm Performance and Share Prices
affiliations: University at Buffalo (SUNY) - School of Management and State University of New York at Buffalo - School of Management

detail.title: Augmentation Versus Substitution: Asymmetric Effects of Generative AI on Firm Performance and Share Prices
detail.abstract: How does generative AI affect firm value? We develop a theoretical framework that distinguishes two channels: augmentation, where AI enhances human productivity while preserving firm-specific knowledge, and substitution, where AI replaces human labor but may erode differentiation rents. The model predicts that augmentation unambiguously increases firm value, whereas substitution has ambiguous effects because cost savings can be offset by the standardization of previously scarce expertise. To test these predictions, we score 18,796 O*NET task descriptions using a large language model along both dimensions, aggregate the scores by occupation using importance weights, and map them to firms using industry employment shares. Exploiting the release of ChatGPT as an information shock in a difference-in-differences framework, we document a sharp asymmetry across tests. Augmentation exposure is associated with significant improvements in operating profitability, labor productivity, and risk-adjusted abnormal returns; substitution exposure shows null effects on returns and negative effects on profitability. A long–short portfolio sorted on augmentation delivers a five-factor alpha of 97 basis points per month, while the corresponding substitution portfolio earns zero alpha. Short sellers reduce positions in high-augmentation firms and increase them in high-substitution firms, consistent with informed investors recognizing the asymmetry. We further show that a novel Knowledge Utilization Intensity measure—capturing the degree to which occupations rely on scarce, cognitively demanding expertise—produces the same return and profitability patterns, confirming that augmentation creates value through complementarity with knowledge-intensive human capital. A functional channel decomposition identifies information processing as the primary AI capability driving the augmentation premium, with effects traceable from operating fundamentals through to asset prices.

detail.title: Mobility Impacts of Ending Telework: Traffic Speed Changes Following the Federal Return-to-Office Mandate near Redstone Arsenal, Huntsville, Alabama
detail.abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic demonstrated that widespread telework can substantially reduce traffic congestion, yet no empirical study has examined the reverse: how traffic conditions respond when remote work is abruptly eliminated. This study exploits the January 2025 federal Return-to-Office (RTO) mandate, which required over two million U.S. federal employees to resume full-time in-person work, as a natural experiment to measure traffic speed impacts on commuter corridors near Redstone Arsenal in Huntsville, Alabama, a quintessentially auto-dependent region with approximately 45,000 federal and contractor personnel and virtually no transit alternatives to absorb returning commuters. Using INRIX speed data collected at 5-minute intervals from 14 road segments across five Arsenal gate corridors, a before-after analysis was conducted across three 15-day study windows: Pre-Order (January 6–20), During-Order (February 10–24), and Post-Order (March 10–24, 2025). A dynamic rush-hour detection algorithm identified period-specific congestion windows, and both rush-hour and full 24-hour speed profiles were evaluated using Welch’s t-tests and Cohen’s d effect sizes. Results revealed pronounced spatial heterogeneity: Gate 9 (Rideout Road, the Arsenal’s main entrance) showed PM speed declines of 21.2 MPH (Cohen’s d = 10.8, p < 0.001), while Gate 7, serving lighter traffic, showed no significant changes in any comparison, providing informal spatial control evidence against regional confounding. Speed reductions followed a temporal gradient aligned with commuter traffic intensity (PM Rush > AM Rush, Midday > Night), and impacts intensified from the During-Order to the Post-Order period, with all 24 hours eventually showing speed reductions. Post-Order effects extended beyond rush hours into midday and shoulder periods, consistent with peak spreading. These findings provide the first empirical evidence that the congestion benefits of telework are reversible and concentrated at capacity-constrained bottleneck locations, and demonstrate that in auto-dependent regions, telework may function as the single most effective congestion management tool available.

detail.abstract:
Enterprise adoption of AI governance tools has accelerated across regulated industries, yet methods for evaluating whether those tools produce verifiable compliance evidence remain underdeveloped. Organizations frequently report that AI governance is “in place,” but the architectural properties required to demonstrate per-decision policy authorization are often absent. This paper introduces a structural taxonomy of governance failure modes—governance laundering, policy theater, and five related families—that arise when governance artifacts are mistaken for governance evidence.

We define seven evidence-grade governance requirements (R1–R7) and classify failure modes according to the structural property each violates, including enforcement binding, independence of verification, state completeness, non-delegability, pre-execution authorization, custody continuity, and semantic stability. Building on prior distinctions between visibility, alignment, and authorization layers in AI governance architectures, we formalize the Expanded Anti-Laundering Protocol (EALP), a reproducible seven-test diagnostic framework for determining whether a system produces independently verifiable, per-decision policy evidence.

The paper contributes a definitional boundary between governance artifacts and governance evidence, a structured failure-mode taxonomy, a graded evaluation protocol with worked examples, and an architectural susceptibility mapping across common categories of governance products. The framework is vendor-neutral and architecture-focused; it does not propose a new governance design but provides a methodology for evaluating whether existing systems satisfy evidentiary standards required in regulated environments. Implications for procurement, audit, and regulatory oversight are discussed, along with limitations and directions for empirical benchmarking.

title: Does low-cost carrier penetration always lead to lower airfares? An analysis of the US domestic market from 2018 to 2023

detail.title: Does low-cost carrier penetration always lead to lower airfares? An analysis of the US domestic market from 2018 to 2023
detail.abstract: Understanding how low-cost carrier (LCC) penetration shapes airfare is central to competition policy, airline strategy and welfare analysis. This paper examines how low-cost carrier (LCC) penetration affects airfare dynamics using a large US domestic route–time panel (2018–2023). Employing a control-function two-stage residual-inclusion estimator to address endogeneity, we also incorporate quadratic and interaction terms to capture nonlinear effects and pandemicrelated shifts. Our results show fares decline as LCC share rises, but the relationship is convex: marginal reductions are largest at low penetration and taper at higher levels. During COVID19, pricing power from additional LCC share was weaker at low penetration but slightly stronger at high penetration. These findings suggest the greatest consumer benefits occur when LCCs expand from minimal to moderate presence.

title: Patchwork, Misattention, and Pandering: Theory and Evidence on (Generative) AI Biases in Strategy
affiliations: Leeds School of Business, University of Colorado, Boulder,  and University of Utah

detail.title: Patchwork, Misattention, and Pandering: Theory and Evidence on (Generative) AI Biases in Strategy
detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is often presented as a remedy to human cognitive limitations such as bounded rationality and bias. However, we argue that (generative) AI systemsespecially large language models (LLMs)-exhibit their own systematic biases, grounded not in psychology but in their underlying architecture and training procedures. We identify three key sets of biases in LLMs that constrain their capacity to solve strategic problems: (1) the patchwork bias: the misuse or misapplication of heuristics (or "patches") and the corresponding lack of global coherence; (2) the misattention bias: the tendency to excessively focus on surface cues and biased consensus views at the expense of true root causes and contrarian views; and (3) the pandering bias: the prioritization of agreeable or engaging responses over accurate or original ones. We first discuss the source of these biases, which result directly from the architectural features of LLMs that generate their remarkable capacities. We then conduct and report on empirical demonstrations of each bias in the context of strategic problem solving. We discuss the limitations of existing solutions designed to overcome these biases. Finally, we conclude with a discussion of the implications for strategic problem solving.

detail.title: Institutions, Organizations, and the Bounded Agency Imperative; Rethinking Governance Design in the Age of Agentic AI
detail.abstract: The institutional frameworks through which modern societies govern organizations were developed for a world of human agents: actors whose cognitive limits, organizational roles, and human-tempo decision-making rendered delegation traceable and accountability legible. The rapid diffusion of agentic artificial intelligence alters these underlying conditions. AI systems now exercise delegated authority continuously, adaptively, and at operational speeds that exceed the temporal assumptions embedded in existing institutional oversight mechanisms. This paper argues that this development represents a structural transition requiring the extension and adaptation of foundational frameworks in institutional economics and organizational theory. Drawing on North's distinction between institutions and organizations, the paper introduces bounded agency-the structural requirement that delegated machine initiative be explicitly constrained within limits that institutional mechanisms of responsibility, legitimacy, and enforcement can effectively govern-and contrasts it with Simon's bounded rationality. Where bounded rationality reshaped organizational design around human cognitive limits, bounded agency highlights the institutional design constraints that arise when non-human systems exercise initiative within organizational workflows. Cross-domain analysis shows that sectors such as commercial aviation, space systems, and nuclear operations preserved bounded agency prospectively through architectural authority limits, while algorithmic trading, content moderation, and clinical AI exhibit the structural governance gaps that arise where such limits were not embedded ex ante. The paper establishes the theoretical foundation for bounded agency as a structural condition of AI-mediated delegation and outlines its implications for institutional design in the AI era.

detail.abstract: The debate over stablecoin yield has become the central fault line in U.S. digital asset legislation. The Guiding and Establishing National Innovation for U.S. Stablecoins Act (GENIUS Act), enacted in July 2025, establishes the first federal prudential framework for dollar-backed payment stablecoins and explicitly prohibits issuers from paying interest or yield to token holders. That prohibition reflects the statute's foundational bargain: regulatory clarity in exchange for operating as neutral payment instruments rather than deposit substitutes. This article argues that the statute's exemption for governance-based rewards threatens to hollow out that bargain. By tying distributions to nominal participation in protocol governance, such as casting periodic votes on network proposals, stablecoin platforms may satisfy the formal "identifiable activity" standard while preserving the economic substance of passive yield. Drawing on the Dimon-Witt policy debate, proposed OCC rulemaking, and the October 2025 collapse of Ethena's USDe, the article demonstrates how governance reward structures can replicate prohibited interest payments through technically compliant means. Without a more substantive standard, one that ties governance rewards to demonstrable engagement rather than perfunctory participation, the governance exemption will become a vehicle for regulatory arbitrage that exposes the financial system to the deposit-run dynamics the GENIUS Act was designed to prevent. The article proposes specific regulatory mechanisms, including voting thresholds, diversified proposal requirements, and economic-at-risk provisions, to distinguish genuine decentralized governance from its simulation.

detail.abstract: Family engagement is widely recognised as a critical factor in improving intervention outcomes across social service systems. However, professionals often struggle to effectively engage families, particularly those with complex family dynamics. In Singapore, these challenges are compounded by cultural norms that emphasise emotional restraint and family harmony, as well as practitioners’ reported lack of confidence in systemic family work. In response, the Family-Centred Approach (FCA) was developed to promote contextual, relational, and strength-based engagement. FCA centres on Adapt, Relational, and Asset-Oriented (ARA) strategies, delivered through structured training and ongoing consultation. This pilot study evaluated the preliminary effectiveness of FCA training among 12 psychologists. Statistically significant improvements were observed in self-reported confidence, competence, and sustainability of family engagement practices, with moderate to large effect sizes, supported by supplementary administrative data. Although participants’ fidelity scores across domains showed non-significant improvements, the observed shifts in self-reported practice and service delivery patterns suggested that FCA holds promise as a feasible and effective framework. The success of the implementation was likely driven by the training programme’s integration of didactic teaching, experiential learning, and reflective consultations, which supported skill acquisition, contextual adaptation, and sustained application. FCA’s emphasis on practical frameworks, cultural responsiveness, and role-relevant tailoring also enabled practitioners to shift from individual-centric to family-centric engagement, even within high-demand settings. While family-level engagement outcomes were not directly measured, these practitioner-level improvements suggest that FCA may facilitate more family-centred practice, highlighting its potential for broader application and scaling across Singapore’s social service ecosystem.

detail.abstract: Holding cash has a cost. For an EPS-maximizing CEO, that cost equals her firm's earnings yield. EPS maximizers retain cash when they can get an even higher yield by investing the money. Otherwise, they return cash to shareholders. This is the EPS-maximizing payout policy. Growth stocks (EY < rf) never return cash because they can clear their low earnings-yield hurdle by investing in riskfree bonds. Value stocks (EY > rf) face a higher hurdle, which makes cash their cheapest source of capital but also raises the opportunity cost of retention. Value stocks return cash when they cannot invest in enough high-yield projects to make up for the higher cost. Paradoxically, the firms that are most likely to distribute cash—deep value stocks (EY >> rf)—are also the ones for whom internal cash is cheapest relative to external financing. Dividends and buybacks both deliver the same value to shareholders, but only buybacks can be accretive. Hence, EPS-maximizing CEOs prefer to distribute via buybacks. Some firms pay dividends for reasons outside our model. Such departures should concentrate among marginal value stocks (EY ≈ rf) where the accretive pull of buybacks is weakest. Empirically, this logic explains which firms return cash, how they distribute the money, and time-series trends.

detail.abstract:
Across institutions, technologies, and knowledge environments, systems increasingly remain operational while producing outcomes that feel hollow, performative, or disconnected from reality. Metrics improve even as results degrade, language remains fluent as meaning erodes, and individuals experience cognitive exhaustion and disorientation without obvious error, deception, or collapse. Existing explanations such as corruption, misinformation, misaligned incentives, or information overload capture surface symptoms. However, they fail to identify a unifying structural mechanism.

This paper proposes Reality Drift, a theory of representational failure in scaled symbolic systems. The core claim is that, as symbolic systems expand and optimize, their representations drift away from reality faster than corrective constraints can bind them. This drift is gradual, non-intentional, and self-reinforcing. Systems continue to function, but meaning detaches. Optimization replaces reference and symbols circulate autonomously. As a result, human cognition adapts at increasing cost.

The paper introduces a five-operator explanatory grammar consisting of drift, constraint, compression, representation, and filtering. Together these describe how the condition emerges and persists across domains. The theory generates testable predictions for institutions, artificial intelligence, and human cognition while providing a structural diagnosis of how meaning degrades under scale.

This paper introduces R Gate™—a rail‑agnostic governance primitive that withholds or releases finance‑visible modernization benefits only upon evidence of stress‑durable performance. We define stress durability as the degree to which improvements in timing predictability, straight‑through processing, and exception recovery remain intact during peak loads, outage recovery, cross‑border cutovers, and multi‑rail interactions. We locate stress durability in a finance‑first transmission chain—Modernization → (if durable) Friction Reduction → Risk Premia → Discount Rate → Valuation—clarifying why attractive pilot medians do not justify changing buffers or discount‑rate inputs absent stress‑validated persistence. All constructs are conceptual and non‑enabling; no decision logic, mappings, or numerical criteria are disclosed. R Gate™ complements, and is separable from, Part I (TVP™), which frames the finance‑first pathway from modernization to valuation without implementation detail.

detail.abstract: Despite the widely accepted view that foot pursuits are inherently dangerous for both police officers and citizens, a minority of municipal police agencies have adopted policies that have the potential to minimize the risk of harm by limiting the circumstances in which police officers are permitted to pursue a subject on foot. This paper presents data related to foot pursuit incidents and existing foot pursuit policies. The paper documents that most existing foot pursuit policies are limited in their potential to reduce unwarranted deadly encounters because the guidance they provide requires officers to consider and weigh vague concepts in tense, urgent situations. Existing policies also afford officers overly broad discretion in deciding whether to initiate and when to terminate a foot pursuit. The paper also presents an analysis of foot pursuit incidents that culminate in the use of deadly force. The data collected and analyzed illustrate that a substantial proportion of these incidents involve circumstances for which most policies suggest the pursuit should not have been initiated or should have been terminated. The analysis supports the premise that broader adoption of foot pursuit policies as well as streamlining and tightening existing policies could reduce the number of foot pursuits that occur, thereby diminishing potential harm to officers and citizens. Additionally, the analysis identifies a critical gap in existing foot pursuit policy content. The data confirms that a significant proportion of foot pursuits ending in deadly force involve subjects that are either perceived to be armed or are armed in fact. This is a challenging circumstance for officers that is left unaddressed by a majority of existing policies.

This paper explores how advanced Natural Language Processing (NLP) techniques, including topic modeling and transformer-based models, can enhance the SLR process by identifying latent thematic structures and uncovering conceptual relationships. We introduce a six-step NLP-driven framework for SLRs that is both scalable and replicable, enabling the identification of emerging trends, refinement of theoretical constructs, and bridging of interdisciplinary knowledge gaps. Our approach not only automates the literature synthesis process but also deepens theoretical insights, offering a methodological advancement for scholars conducting reviews in dynamic research fields. The findings underscore the potential of NLP-driven SLRs to transform management research by enhancing efficiency, rigor, and theoretical integration.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the persistence of historical repetition as a consequence of collective and individual psychological structures rather than a lack of historical knowledge. Drawing on Gustave Le Bon’s theory of crowd psychology, the study argues that collective experience does not generate durable learning, as the psychological mechanisms governing mass behavior remain invariant across time. detail.abstract: This book examines an under-theorized but widespread governance condition in small nonprofit and charitable organizations: extreme role compression, in which a single individual simultaneously occupies executive, governance, administrative, operational, and representational roles that are formally intended to be separated. Drawing on an anonymized case study of a community-based charity, the book argues that role compression is not merely a matter of poor governance practice or individual overreach, but a structural adaptation to resource scarcity, board passivity, regulatory complexity, and funder expectations. While nonprofit law, governance manuals, and professional training programs presume a functioning division of authority between board and management, this case demonstrates how such assumptions routinely collapse in small organizations that lack staff, engaged directors, or stable funding. The result is a governance paradox: the individual most responsible for sustaining the organization also becomes exposed to heightened legal, financial, and personal risk, while the board's fiduciary role becomes largely symbolic. By situating this case within nonprofit governance theory, fiduciary law, and the literature on executive compensation and oversight, the book shows how role compression blurs the boundaries between volunteerism and paid labor, accountability and autonomy, legality and necessity. The book contributes a conceptual framework for understanding role compression as a distinct governance pathology, analyzes its consequences for organizational legitimacy and sustainability, and offers normative and policy-oriented implications for boards, regulators, and funders who continue to rely on governance models ill-suited to the realities of small charities.

detail.abstract: Does digital infrastructure accelerate trade integration in Africa? This paper examines whether digital readiness amplifies the trade effects of the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA). Using a balanced panel of 47 African economies (2012-2024), we construct a composite Digital Readiness Index via Principal Component Analysis and estimate a continuous difference-indifferences model with Driscoll-Kraay standard errors to account for cross-sectional dependence. We evaluate impacts across three outcome layers; total trade openness, trade in services, and ICT service export share. The results reveal a striking structural divergence. While digital readiness has no significant impact on aggregate merchandise trade (b = 6.71, p > .10), it acts as a robust catalyst for the service sector. Specifically, a one-standard-deviation increase in digital readiness is associated with an 18.9 percentage point increase in service trade openness (p < .01) in the post-AfCFTA period. Placebo tests using a fictitious policy year (2017) confirm the causal validity of these estimates (p = .119), while heterogeneity analysis finds no systematic differential effects across income groups (p > .10). These findings suggest that AfCFTA's early digital dividends materialize exclusively in services rather than goods, highlighting the urgency of the Protocol on Digital Trade to unlock broader export diversification.

detail.title: Clearing Multi-Unit Markets with Simple Pricing
detail.abstract: We study multi-unit markets where a seller allocates multiple units of an item to buyers with different valuation functions via simple pricing. When the valuation functions are submodular, a Walrasian equilibrium with a single (per-unit) price exists, i.e., each buyer obtains an allocation that maximizes her utility and the market clears. However, market clearing may fail, and a Walrasian equilibrium might not exist even under slight deviations from submodularity. To study how such equilibria can be approximated for more general classes of valuations, we introduce the τ-approximate Walrasian equilibrium: a market-clearing allocation and a single price for which each buyer's utility is not necessarily maximum, but it is weakly larger than the maximum utility under τ-scaled valuations. We establish that any τ-approximate Walrasian equilibrium guarantees at least a τ-fraction of the optimal social welfare, which motivates our main question: what is the tightest approximation of the Walrasian equilibrium achievable with a single price? We provide a Pseudo-Polynomial Time Approximation Scheme (PPTAS) that finds the tightest approximation for general valuation functions. Furthermore, for single-peaked marginal valuation functions, which generalizes both submodular and supermodular valuation functions, we utilize the demand structure to design Fully Polynomial-Time Approximation Scheme (FPTAS). We go beyond a single price and, interestingly, establish a structural separation: while a single anonymous price suffices for single-minded buyers, non-anonymous pricing (specifically, offering distinct per-unit prices to two buyer groups) is necessary to find the tightest relaxation for buyers with general single-peaked marginal valuations.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the evolving landscape of cryptocurrency-related illicit finance and political influence in the United States. While Bitcoin historically dominated narratives about cryptoenabled crime, recent data reveals that stablecoins now represent 84% of illicit transaction volume, driven by their price stability and low transaction costs. Despite this shift, blockchain transparency has enabled sophisticated law enforcement capabilities, with analytics firms successfully tracing and recovering billions in stolen assets. Simultaneously, stablecoins have achieved genuine product-market fit, processing over $10 trillion monthly in legitimate payments. However, the cryptocurrency industry's transformation into a major political force, exemplified by $193 million in campaign spending and ventures like World Liberty Financial, raises serious concerns about regulatory capture and democratic accountability. This analysis provides business academics with a nuanced understanding of digital assets that acknowledges both their functional innovation and profound ethical challenges.

detail.abstract: For the last decade, the prevailing way to describe our relationship with AI has been “human–AI interaction.” It sounds reasonable: a person uses a system, the system responds, the person decides. But the essence of that relationship is rapidly changing and call it an interaction is misleading because it implies that AI sits outside the flow of work and thought, waiting to be “interacted with.” That’s not what is happening anymore. What is rapidly emerging is what I call “human-AI integration”. It is a condition where AI is embedded into everyday cognition, workflows, decision routines, and increasingly permeating organizational governance. The unit of change is no longer “a user interacting with a machine or a digital tool.” It is the reconfiguration of how work gets done—and how judgment, accountability, and capability are distributed across people and machines which are smart, connected and becoming increasingly autonomous. Let’s dig further into it.

detail.abstract: This paper revisits the Arab-Israeli conflict as a moral and ethical problem shaped not only by territory or security, but by competing historical memories, asymmetric power, and the selective application of international law. Rather than reducing the conflict to moral binaries or contemporary flashpoints, the analysis situates present-day violence within longer histories of colonial governance, displacement, and trauma, examining how the Holocaust and the Nakba have been mobilized as competing moral reference points that structure political legitimacy and ethical recognition. Drawing on international humanitarian law, political philosophy, and global ethical discourse, the paper argues that historical suffering, while demanding acknowledgment, cannot function as a permanent exemption from accountability. It examines how legal frameworks, security narratives, and media representations have contributed to the normalization of civilian harmparticularly in Gaza-while fragmenting international ethical consensus. By treating memory as a form of power rather than solely as inheritance, the paper contends that moral fracture persists when history is invoked to justify asymmetry rather than constrain it. The analysis concludes that peace cannot be grounded in selective ethics or narrative dominance; without accountability, recognition, and restraint, memory itself becomes a source of continued injustice rather than reconciliation. The paper adopts an international, ethics-forward perspective grounded in political philosophy and humanitarian law, treating the conflict not as an isolated dispute but as a case study in selective moral recognition and the limits of historical justification. detail.abstract: This paper examines whether breaking the law can be morally justified-and at times morally required-when legal systems perpetuate injustice rather than constrain it. Challenging the assumption that legality and morality are synonymous, the analysis situates resistance within moral philosophy, political theory, and historical practice, arguing that ethical legitimacy depends not on obedience alone but on the alignment between law, dignity, and justice. By situating resistance within the ethical conditions of 2025, the analysis concludes that when law ceases to protect dignity, moral courage may require refusal-not as heroism, but as obligation. detail.abstract: Government spending correlates with lobbying intensity, not marginal societal value.
