The recent enactment of the Investment and Securities Act 2025 has brought about a major  policy shift in the Nigerian stock market. It now seeks to integrate digital assets into Nigeria’s capital market framework by classifying certain digital assets as securities and placing them under the supervision of the Securities and Exchange Commission thus, no longer treating them as anomalies outside existing financial law.

This piece attempts to query the standards for this absorption and recommend setting steps necessary to save regulators in the Finance Industry from experiencing conflicts as their administer their respective roles.

title: The Gist of It: The Uneasy Triangle of Sports Journalism, Deadlines & Defamation Law
affiliations: and Independent

detail.title: The Gist of It: The Uneasy Triangle of Sports Journalism, Deadlines & Defamation Law

publicationDetails.detailsText: Harvard Journal of Sports and Entertainment Law, Vol. 17 (forthcoming, 2026)

detail.abstract:
The Article examines how today’s fast-paced media environment, especially in sports journalism, increases the likelihood of reporting errors and complicates defamation law. 

Using two cases—Spears v. New York Times (a former Alabama athlete allegedly misidentified as present at a fatal shooting) and a similar claim by former Stanford football coach Troy Taylor against ESPN (for allegedly exaggerated bullying accusations)—it analyzes how media defendants rely on the doctrine of substantial truth, which protects technically inaccurate statements if the “gist” or “sting” of the reporting is deemed accurate. 

The Article questions whether this doctrine, together with broad public figure rules, is appropriate in an era of “process journalism,” where stories are published quickly and repeatedly updated, and where public distrust of “fake news” is already high.

Against a backdrop of collapsing public trust in traditional media, the rise of social media misinformation, and the growing use of error-prone AI tools in news production and aggregation, the Article argues that the law should do more to promote accuracy. 

The Article urges media organizations to prioritize getting stories right over breaking them first and calls on courts to apply substantial truth more cautiously and to narrow the definition of who counts as a public figure—particularly as college athletes gain NIL income, social media followings, and quasi-celebrity status. 

These reforms, the Article contends, would better protect individuals from reputational harm, respond to the distorted dynamics of algorithmic amplification, and reduce legal uncertainty for responsible journalism while reinforcing democratic trust.

title: A point so fundamental: Nozick on intellectual property
affiliations: New York University School of Law

detail.title: A point so fundamental: Nozick on intellectual property

publicationDetails.detailsText: Critical Review of International Social and Political Philosophy, 0[10.1080/13698230.2026.2630588]

detail.abstract: In Anarchy, State and Utopia, Nozick defends a libertarian theory of property rights under a minimal state. Whether libertarian theory supports or excludes intellectual property (IP) rights remains controversial. This paper shows that, although Nozick only mentions intellectual property (IP) a few times in the book, these discussions turn out to be surprisingly pivotal for his arguments. Indeed, Nozick calls IP rights a 'fundamental' issue for libertarian theory. So, it is important to analyse the structural, methodological, and substantive implications of what Nozick says (and does not say) about IP rights. I will show that in Part 1 of ASU, IP rights illustrate the non-ideal problem of persistent disagreement, which shows that the minimal state cannot simply administer justice; it must also tackle disagreements about the content of justice. In Part 2 of ASU, Nozick discusses patents to illustrate the limits of the Lockean Proviso. His embrace of counterfactual reasoning opens the surprising possibility that even property rights in physical resources may be up for time limitations, inheritance laws, or other proviso-motivated regulations. Overall, Nozick's discussion of IP rights illuminates the somewhat neglected role of non-ideal libertarian theory, epistemic indeterminacy, counterfactual reasoning, and pragmatic, 'rule-of-thumb' remedies in ASU. In the final analysis, Nozick does not develop a fully coherent picture of IP rights, and his proposed solution, putting time limits on patents, seems somewhat ad hoc. Although IP rights play an underappreciated role in the book, his discussion raises more questions than it answers. The epistemically humble libertarian (or liberal) should approach the regulation of IP rights, and other thorny issues of real-world propertyownership, with an open mind.

title: Enforcing the Community Reinvestment Act
affiliations: University of Michigan, Stephen M. Ross School of Business and University of Michigan Law School

detail.title: Enforcing the Community Reinvestment Act

publicationDetails.detailsText: U of Michigan Law & Econ Research Paper No. 25-036
publicationDetails.journalName: University of Michigan Law School, Law & Economics Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Nearly fifty years after the Community Reinvestment Act of 1977 (CRA) required banks to serve low- and moderate-income (LMI) areas, the systematic exclusion of disadvantaged communities from the mainstream financial system persists. This Article identifies a novel explanation for the CRA's limited impact: its enforcement mechanisms are ineffective.

The CRA operates through two enforcement channels. Regulators must (1) consider a bank's CRA record when the bank seeks permission to merge or expand, and (2) publish periodic assessments of each bank's CRA performance. Using twenty years of CRA data, we show that neither enforcement mechanism works as intended. Banks strategically increase CRA lending before announcing mergers, then sharply curtail it after obtaining regulatory approval. Meanwhile, public disclosure of CRA ratings--either good or bad--has no discernible effect on banks' financial performance. These findings indicate that the CRA's enforcement mechanisms do not encourage banks to make long-term, sustained investments in LMI communities as intended.

Our results suggest that policymakers should fundamentally rethink CRA enforcement. We propose reforms that regulators could implement within the existing statutory framework, such as evaluating banks' historical CRA ratings during merger reviews, enhancing public disclosure requirements, and adopting new incentives for strong performance. Given the persistence of financial exclusion in the United States, we also evaluate alternative strategies beyond the current statutory framework that could better promote equitable access to the financial system. We examine approaches used successfully in other countries, such as universal service mandates and public banking, that could complement or replace the CRA to help ensure underserved communities have access to basic financial services.

title: Beyond Ratification: Kosovo's Unique Path to Safeguarding Human Dignity and Fundamental Rights
affiliations: Albanian University and Office of Prime Minister (Kosovo)

detail.title: Beyond Ratification: Kosovo's Unique Path to Safeguarding Human Dignity and Fundamental Rights

publicationDetails.detailsText: Bulletin of the Transilvania University of Braşov. Series VII: Social Sciences • Law, 2026[10.31926/but.ssl.2025.18.67.3.37]

detail.abstract: Amidst the ongoing efforts to become a full member of the international community, the Republic of Kosovo applies a temporary yet effective approach for safeguarding human dignity and fundamental rights: providing, via its Constitution, direct applicability to nine notable international human rights instruments, the latest being the Istanbul Convention in 2020. In this paper, we analyze the feasibility of this model and its application in practice. By essentially mirroring UN and CoE human rights standards, the Republic of Kosovo offers a unique case on protecting human rights, while still being a member of neither organization. This fact alone should qualify the state for membership in both.

title: Clauses with Claws: Reducing Agency Costs in Late-Merging SPACs
affiliations: University of Oklahoma - Michael F. Price College of Business

detail.title: Clauses with Claws: Reducing Agency Costs in Late-Merging SPACs
detail.abstract: Existing theory predicts that deadline driven agency distortions arise even under optimal contracting. We show that ex-ante contract design can substantially attenuate these distortions in practice. Leveraging the unique institutional features of special purpose acquisition companies (SPACs), we re-examine the relationship between economic contracting and merger outcomes. We find that contingency clauses can mitigate high agency costs that become especially pronounced near the SPAC liquidation deadline by aligning manager and shareholder interests. Late merging SPACs without such clauses underperform, with 9-11% lower merger announcement returns and 19% lower post-merger ROA. Notably, SPAC contingency clauses are only performative when agency costs are high, underscoring their importance in improving the quality of late SPAC mergers. These results provide a channel by which SPACs can be constructed to minimize agency costs born of the SPAC structure, informing regulatory policy.

title: Redesigning the classical automatic selection of X-11 seasonal filters
affiliations: Deutsche Bundesbank

detail.title: Redesigning the classical automatic selection of X-11 seasonal filters
detail.abstract: The classical X-11 seasonal adjustment method for monthly and quarterly time series is equipped with routines for data-driven selections of both Henderson trend-cycle filters and 3 × k seasonal moving averages, currently involving up to three candidate filters in either case. Although these routines have a long-standing tradition that can be traced back at least to 1960, they have not been adopted in a recent JDemetra+ implementation of a modified X-11 method tailored to the specifics of infra-monthly time series, such as the coexistence of multiple seasonal patterns with potentially fractional periodicities. Focusing on seasonal moving averages, we seek to fill this gap by suggesting a generic redesign of the legacy selection concept based upon the so-called moving seasonality ratio. This blueprint utilises a broader set of candidate seasonal filters and, unlike the original setting, a set of common approaches for deriving the requisite asymmetric variants. Considering intersections of multiple approach-specific selection rules stabilises the final filter choice and, what is more, naturally provides the warranted thresholds controlling the potential recalculation of the moving seasonality ratio from suitably shortened detrended observations. Our proposed redesign is illustrated using one specific rule based upon threshold quartiles and real-time data for three German macroeconomic time series sampled at quarterly, monthly, and daily intervals. The last example also highlights the need for additional intermediate steps in the calculation of the moving seasonality ratio when the data contain complex seasonal dynamics.

title: Prompt Governance in Financial AI: Comparative Performance of Structured Frameworks in Insurance and Investment Tasks

detail.title: Prompt Governance in Financial AI: Comparative Performance of Structured Frameworks in Insurance and Investment Tasks

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the creator of the ACTFIT framework and founder of Finantor, a personal financial management company with AI. To mitigate potential bias, all experimental materials (prompts, datasets, source code, raw scores, and human validation form) are publicly available at https://github.com/hirbis/prompt-governance for independent verification. Results include findings that do not favor ACTFIT (hallucination rate higher than Few-shot; accuracy advantage over Few-shot not statistically significant) and negative findings about an alternative framework (CRISPE), reported with equal transparency.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in high-stakes financial domains, yet their output stability and factual reliability remain central concerns. We present the first systematic benchmark of four prompt governance approaches (Baseline zero-shot, Few-shot, CRISPE, and ACTFIT) across two representative financial tasks: life insurance risk classification and investment portfolio allocation. Using three commercial LLMs (Claude Sonnet 4.5, GPT-4.1, and Gemini 2.5 Flash), we evaluate 60 simulated cases through 2,160 API calls, measuring accuracy, hallucination rate, cross-run consistency, and a composite Efficiency Score. Evaluation employs two independent LLM judges from different model families (Claude Opus 4.6 and GPT-4o) with inter-rater agreement of κ = 0.97 for accuracy, validated by a stratified human sample (n = 98, κ = 0.82 judge-human). ACTFIT achieves 67.0% accuracy versus 44.9% for the baseline (+22.1pp), with particularly pronounced effects on investment tasks (+46.1pp). ACTFIT yields the highest Efficiency Score (0.537 vs. 0.342 baseline, +56.8%). GPT-4.1 combined with ACTFIT reaches the dataset peak: 81.7% accuracy with 0% hallucination at US$ 0.006 per correct response. CRISPE produces a surprising negative finding: accuracy below the baseline (41.1% vs. 44.9%) with a 49.1% hallucination rate, demonstrating that poorly designed governance degrades performance. Our findings suggest that institutional prompt governance offers a cost-effective alternative to fine-tuning for financial applications, with implications for regulatory compliance and operational risk management.

title: The Unnecessary Agency
affiliations: ,  and University of Minnesota Law School

detail.title: The Unnecessary Agency
detail.abstract:
Recently, the U.S. Government has reduced the power of federal agencies. The Supreme Court has shifted power from agencies to courts by, among other things, eliminating Chevron deference and curtailing agency authority to issue civil penalties. Moreover, the Trump administration has expressed interest in streamlining agencies in order to eliminate redundancy and waste. 

In this time of rethinking the balance of power between federal agencies and courts, the U.S. International Trade Commission’s (ITC’s) role in intellectual property law is outdated. Decades ago, Congress granted the ITC the power to investigate acts of IP infringement along with the authority to grant exclusion orders prohibiting the importation of articles that infringe U.S. patents. However, most of the original rationales that supported the ITC’s broad jurisdiction over infringing articles have fallen by the wayside, as federal district courts now have jurisdiction to hear almost all (if not all) IP disputes that are currently brought before the ITC. Although the ITC remains an attractive forum for patent holders, the duplicative system of ITC and district court litigation is costly for both domestic businesses and the public. This duplication also creates intractable conflicts between judicial and administrative patent law decisions.

Accordingly, we propose that Congress revoke the ITC’s jurisdiction over IP infringement cases and grant the federal district courts in rem jurisdiction over infringing articles imported into the United States. Such legislation would maintain the advantages that make ITC patent suits attractive to patent holders, while greatly reducing the costs of patent enforcement and rationalizing the substantive and procedural law applicable in patent disputes.

title: High-Frequency Instruments with Time-Varying Reliability: Understanding Identification in Macroeconomics
affiliations: ,  and Deutsche Bundesbank - Research Centre

detail.title: High-Frequency Instruments with Time-Varying Reliability: Understanding Identification in Macroeconomics
detail.abstract: The effects of monetary policy shocks are regularly estimated using high-frequency surprises in asset prices around central bank meetings as an instrument. These studies, insofar as they explicitly model the relationship between instrument and structural shock, assume a constant relationship between the instrument and the monetary policy shock. By allowing for time variation in this relationship, we show that only a few distinct periods are informative about monetary policy shocks. Therefore, we build a narrative for instrument-based identification. For the instrument in Gertler & Karadi (2015), the effect on the (log) price level is almost 50 percent larger than the standard specification would suggest.

title: Differential Market Responses to Infrastructure vs Regulatory Events in Cryptocurrency Markets

detail.title: Differential Market Responses to Infrastructure vs Regulatory Events in Cryptocurrency Markets

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflict of interest.

detail.abstract: We investigate differential market responses to infrastructure versus regulatory events in cryptocurrency markets using event study methodology with 4-category event classification. From 50 candidate events (2019-2025), 31 meet inclusion criteria across Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana, and Cardano. We employ constant mean and market-adjusted models with event-level block bootstrap confidence intervals that properly account for cross-sectional correlation. Our primary comparison focuses on negative-valence events: infrastructure failures (8 events) versus regulatory enforcement (7 events). Infrastructure failures produce mean Cumulative Abnormal Return (CAR) of-7.6% (95% CI: [-25.8%, +11.3%]) and regulatory enforcement produces mean CAR of-11.1% (CI: [-31.0%, +10.7%]). The difference of +3.6 percentage points has CI [-25.3%, +30.9%], p = 0.81-a null finding indicating markets respond similarly to both shock types when controlling for valence. Robustness checks confirm consistent results across window specifications, leave-one-out exclusion of major events (FTX, Terra), and alternative market model specifications. The 4category classification addresses prior conflation of upgrades with failures. This exploratory analysis should be treated as hypothesis-generating.

detail.abstract: Strategic interaction under extinction risk is constrained by sequential credibility and non-degenerate termination. An action-dependent hazard induces an equilibrium transition, converting the one-shot temptation into an irreversible shift from a stable environment to a regime of systemic deterioration. This paper derives a threshold that identifies when this regime shift renders grim-trigger sequentially optimal. The dilemma is thereby transformed: cooperation is sustained by the endogenous fragility of the system itself.

detail.abstract: The strategic use of patents within marketing and advertising has emerged as a potent tool as companies vie for consumer attention in competitive markets. This chapter observes the evolving use of patents as a component of advertising strategy across a range of industries and how they impact purchase decisions. It argues that patents serve not only as legal protections but also as instruments for enhancing specific product credibility. By actively communicating patent protection to the market, companies seek to underscore their commitment to innovation and foster consumer trust. In this context, the patent operates beyond its traditional legal function, contributing to brand reputation and perceived transparency. In other words, such intellectual property right transcends its legal role by elevating the reputation of a brand.

detail.abstract: Considering the need for evidence on the overall economic burden of injuries in Low-or Middle-Income Countries (LMICs) for healthcare planning, this study aimed to identify, summarise, and critique the available evidence on the burden of economic costs of sustaining moderate-to severe-injuries in LMICs. This systematic review was conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis (PRISMA) guidelines. A comprehensive literature search was conducted across multiple relevant databases. Inclusion criteria were: publication between 1 January 1995 and 19 July 2024, without language restrictions, conducted in LMICs, and reported original findings on the costs of all moderate-to severe-injuries. Studies reporting only on costs of specific injury types were excluded. Included publications were systematically screened, data extracted, and quality assessed by two reviewers independently. All costs were standardised to the 2023 US$ exchange rate. From the 4782 studies identified, 20 were included for data extraction.

title: The Monist Doctrine As A Catalyst For Integration In Africa

detail.title: The Monist Doctrine As A Catalyst For Integration In Africa

publicationDetails.detailsText: Minnesota Journal of International Law, Issue 2, Vol. 35.

detail.abstract: The African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) aspires to establish a unified market across Africa, integrating approximately 1.2 billion people and generating a cumulative Gross Domestic Product (GDP) exceeding US $3.4 trillion. A key challenge in this endeavor is the legal divergence among African nations, particularly the coexistence of monist and dualist legal systems, which affects the domestication and implementation of international treaties. In dualist jurisdictions, international treaties require domestic legislative enactment before assuming legal force, a process that often results in delays and inconsistencies. Conversely, under the monist doctrine, international agreements acquire immediate domestic applicability, eliminating the need for supplementary legislative procedures. This article critically evaluates the legal, institutional, and procedural challenges associated with a shift towards monism, highlighting the broader implications for regional integration and economic cooperation. Although empirical research linking monism directly to improved regional integration remains limited, this article argues that monist states may have a comparative advantage in executing international agreements, including trade and investment accords under the AfCFTA. The integration of international law seamlessly into domestic legal orders can facilitate policy coordination, reduce bureaucratic obstacles, and promote efficient legal integration within the AfCFTA framework. Using doctrinal and comparative constitutional analysis, the article examines treaty reception and judicial practice in Ghana and Nigeria as paradigmatic dualist jurisdictions, and contrasts them with Kenya's post-2010 constitutional approach, which grants ratified treaties direct domestic effect subject to constitutional limits. The comparison shows how reception design shapes the speed, coherence, and justiciability of AfCFTA commitments, particularly in areas such as customs administration, regulatory cooperation, and dispute settlement-related obligations. The article contributes a legally grounded account of why post-ratification veto points embedded in domestic constitutional systems impede continental harmonization and proposes a reform pathway toward functional monism for integration instruments. The article concludes by proposing key legal and policy reforms necessary for Ghana, Kenya, and Nigeria to transition toward a monist framework. These recommendations aim to optimize the implementation of AfCFTA provisions and contribute to the broader objective of deepening economic integration across Africa.

title: Introduction to Human Nature Institutionalism (Working Paper) -A New Paradigm of Institutional Dynamics Based on the Axiom of Myopic Human Nature Author Information

detail.title: Introduction to Human Nature Institutionalism (Working Paper) -A New Paradigm of Institutional Dynamics Based on the Axiom of Myopic Human Nature Author Information
detail.abstract:
Existing institutional studies are trapped in two dilemmas: the "rational man" assumption deviates from real-world human behavior, and the "pendulum effect" in governance lacks a quantitative explanation, while "pie-in-the-sky institutions" (long-term vague commitments) frequently fail. To address these gaps, this paper proposes a new paradigm of institutional dynamics based on the Axiom of Myopic Human Nature—a cross-culturally universal assumption that humans prioritize immediate interests driven by profit-seeking and loss-aversion, with institutional influence weakening as time delay increases.
We construct a complete theoretical system including "three theorems and two lemmas": ① The Force Attenuation Theorem formalizes the "anti-pie-in-the-sky" mechanism, proving that institutional force decays exponentially with time delay (t) and is quantified by F=k×V×e−αt, verified by failed long-term welfare policies and successful immediate-incentive cases (e.g., the Household Responsibility System in China, the Marshall Plan in the U.S.). ② The Institutional Swing Theorem integrates attenuation effects into a nonlinear Van der Pol limit cycle model, revealing the endogenous mechanism of "self-excitation (long-term institutional attenuation → rule-breaking) → forced restoration (immediate institutional reinforcement → suppression)", supported by cross-cultural cases (Zhu Yuanzhang's anti-corruption, U.S. trade policy swings). ③ The Institutional Efficiency Theorem demonstrates that efficiency E=R0cosθe−αtλC0(1+sinθ) is negatively correlated with both the angle θ (between institutional and human vectors) and attenuation coefficient α, and positively correlated with the completeness of constraint mechanisms (Watermelon-Cutting Principle).
A core practical insight derived from the theory is the "Watermelon-Cutting Principle": "He who cuts the watermelon shall not take the first piece". This principle constrains the profit-seeking bias of institutional designers, forcing fair distribution and avoiding deviations from the original institutional purpose—complementing the "anti-pie-in-the-sky" logic to form a closed-loop solution for institutional design.
Key innovations include: ① Embedding "anti-pie-in-the-sky" logic into the core axiom, explaining the root cause of long-term institutional failure. ② Quantifying institutional force attenuation (α=δ×ξ) and confirming cross-cultural universality (cross-cultural δ difference < 0.1). ③ Integrating the "Watermelon-Cutting Principle" to bridge the gap between theoretical models and practical institutional operation. ④ Triangulation validation via historical cases, global big data, and ABM simulation (10,000 heterogeneous agents), supplemented by rigorous mathematical proofs.
Practical implications: The "Golden Rules" (anti-pie-in-the-sky, interest frontloading, cost internalization, dynamic damping, and the Watermelon-Cutting Principle) provide quantifiable tools for global governance. This study reconstructs the human foundation of institutional economics, bridging the gap between normative logic and positive reality, and offering a scientific solution to the pendulum effect and pie-in-the-sky failure in cross-cultural governance.

detail.abstract: We provide the first large-N test of the endogenous ignorance hypothesis: that elites deliberately control cultural and media consumption to foster voter ignorance and capture political power. Using V-Dem data covering 163 countries over 1945-2024, we find that a one-standard-deviation increase in cultural controls is associated with a 0.39 standard-deviation reduction in electoral democracy. Three instrumental-variable strategies yield consistent causal estimates. Mediation analysis shows that about half of the effect operates through voter ignorance. Media indoctrination dominates education-based indoctrination, and the effect decays smoothly over five years. Results are robust across alternative specifications and data sources.

detail.abstract: Bitcoin's fixed supply makes it ill-suited as a monetary base in growing, credit-based economies, a concern salient for fast-growing Asian economies. Using the quantity identity and a stylized illustration, the paper shows that a hard-capped base implies persistent deflation unless velocity rises persistently, raising real debt burdens and weakening stabilization. It distinguishes managed monetary expansion from devaluation and argues that Bitcoin's comparative advantage is as a store-of-value asset.

title: “Big Bang” Tax Reform: Unleashing Growth in the Canadian Economy
affiliations: C.D. Howe Institute, C.D. Howe Institute and C.D. Howe Institute

detail.title: “Big Bang” Tax Reform: Unleashing Growth in the Canadian Economy
detail.abstract:
• Canada’s tax system has contributed to weak economic performance over the past decade, as the country has recorded the slowest per-capita income growth in the G7 while relying heavily on personal and corporate income taxes that impose relatively high economic costs.
  • This report proposes a sweeping, “big bang” reform that would restructure Canada’s tax system to improve growth, reduce distortions, and simplify compliance and administration. At the federal level, it would lower marginal personal income tax rates, introduce an optional simplified $10,000 tax credit to reduce complexity, and overhaul corporate taxation through either a 10 percent “Irish-style” rate with base broadening or a 13 percent distributed profits tax that defers federal taxation on retained earnings until profits are distributed.
  • The reform is designed to be revenue-neutral in the short term. To offset lower income tax rates, it would shift toward less distortionary sources of revenue, including either a modest increase in the GST or the introduction of a new employer-paid payroll tax dedicated to healthcare, thereby reducing reliance on economically harmful income taxation.
  • Over the long run, the reforms could increase non-residential capital by roughly $140 billion and raise GDP by approximately $79 billion (about 2.5 percent), generating more than $26 billion annually in additional tax revenues while preserving Canada’s strong redistributive outcomes.

detail.title: Central Counterparty Management of Liquid and Prefunded Resources

publicationDetails.detailsText: Office of Financial Research Working Paper No. 26-04

detail.abstract: This paper presents a simple analytical framework for understanding aggregate central counterparty (CCP) resource demands. The framework integrates various dimensions of CCP heterogeneity, including outstanding cleared volume, final settlement mechanism, contract turnover rate, underlying price volatility, market liquidity, market concentration, and certain CCP risk-management parameters, such as the extent of resource mutualization. Where available, we present empirical counterparts to these parameters using data from the Committee on Payments and Market Infrastructures (CPMI) and the International Organization of Securities Commissions (IOSCO) Public Quantitative Disclosures (PQDs). Our framework extends previous literature by explicitly considering liquid as well as capital resources, and we conclude with two reflections on CCP liquidity management. First, CCPs with a high turnover of physically settled contracts, such as securities or repurchase agreements (repos), may use liquid resources to help share funding risks associated with default between members. This helps explain the greater degree of resource mutualization at such CCPs and may even provide a motive for common ownership. Second, without sufficient liquid resources to weather large price dislocations, CCPs may be unable to commit to putting members into default in such circumstances. This may limit market discipline for appropriate ex-ante liquidity management by clearing members.

title: Realized Variance Disagreement
affiliations: Hong Kong University of Science & Technology (HKUST) - Department of Information Systems, Business Statistics and Operations Management and

detail.title: Realized Variance Disagreement
detail.abstract: We propose realized variance disagreement as a nonparametric measure of segmentation between equity and options markets over a fixed time interval. Defined as the aggregate difference between diffusive variance components of high-frequency asset returns and their risk-neutral conditional short-term expectations recovered from options expiring at the end of the trading day, this statistic captures realized violations of the fundamental no-arbitrage condition that diffusive variance coincides under the physical and risk-neutral probability measures. We derive a central limit theorem that enables feasible inference on integrated variance disagreement between equity and options markets. We further develop market integration tests that can detect spot and integrated variance disagreements. Empirically, we find evidence for episodes of disagreement between equity and options markets. These periods exhibit mild persistence and differ in magnitude across assets.

title: International Climate Policy as a Potential Game: Strategic Incentives and Path-Dependent Dynamics
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: International Climate Policy as a Potential Game: Strategic Incentives and Path-Dependent Dynamics
detail.abstract: The strategic challenge of climate policy lies in designing international agreements that handle the tensions inherent in managing a global public good, where the uneven distribution of costs and benefits creates incentives for free-riding. While the game-theoretic literature on International Environmental Agreements (IEAs) provides analytical clarity on coalition stability, Integrated Assessment Models (IAMs) capture complex geophysical dynamics but often abstract from strategic incentives. This paper bridges these approaches by embedding a nonlinear, path-dependent geophysical module directly into the utility structure of a dynamic, open-loop game of international climate policy. We show that, despite the complexity introduced by the climate module, the resulting interaction forms a state-transitive weighted potential game, guaranteeing the existence of a pure-strategy Nash Equilibrium. Using this framework, we generate three key insights. First, the classic ``paradox of cooperation" is endogenous to the perception of catastrophic climate economic damage: higher perceived damage can strengthen incentives for cooperation. Second, truncating analysis at 2100 can dramatically underestimate the true strategic incentives for both cooperative and unilateral action, highlighting the importance of long-term foresight. Third, adaptive institutional mechanisms, akin to the ratchet structure of the Paris Agreement, are superior to static long-term commitments in achieving robust and effective climate outcomes. Our results demonstrate that integrating realistic geophysical risk into strategic models provides a tool for understanding and designing climate agreements, offering both theoretical and policy-relevant insights for addressing the global climate challenge.

title: Estimating Worker Complementarity with an Endogenous Technology Model: Evidence from U.S. Occupational Wages
affiliations: Dickinson College and The Alan Turing Institute

detail.title: Estimating Worker Complementarity with an Endogenous Technology Model: Evidence from U.S. Occupational Wages
detail.abstract: This paper develops a theory of endogenous technology where skill-based worker sorting is a central mechanism. In this approach, skills are modeled as tuples of a spe- cialization and a level of ability. Firms maximize profits by combining these tuples to unlock various schemes of returns to scale. In the model, specialization diversity shifts the production function outwards, allowing firms to temporarily overcome decreasing marginal returns while workers seek to cooperate with people of similar ability taking advantage of complementarities. Calibrating this model with U.S. occupational data, we find that our ability estimates replicate occupation wages at the state and national levels and state-level productivity values, as well as a collection of stylized facts about firms. Our empirical strategy allows us to estimate the size of the skill complementar- ity wage premium at the occupation and region level. This process then provides the that value for every unique occupation-state pair. Though we mostly focus on occu- pation specific measures, on average complementarity accounts for approximately 48% of the a worker’s wage while the median complementarity accounts for 31%, indicating significant clustering of high talent.

title: Design Early or Inherit the Crisis: Mass Arbitration in the United States and Collective Arbitration in Brazil
affiliations: University of California, Berkeley - School of Law and University of São Paulo (USP)

detail.title: Design Early or Inherit the Crisis: Mass Arbitration in the United States and Collective Arbitration in Brazil

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no conflicts of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study does not involve human subjects or empirical data.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
When legal systems suppress collective litigation without addressing the conditions that generate collective claims, aggregation pressures do not disappear — they migrate. The rise of mass arbitration in the United States illustrates this dynamic: judicial enforcement of class action waivers displaced formal aggregation without eliminating its underlying drivers, producing coordinated waves of individualized arbitration demands that strained institutions designed for bilateral dispute resolution. This was not a retreat from arbitration doctrine, but an institutional stress test under conditions of scale.

This Article uses that experience to examine Brazil, where analogous pressures are emerging — particularly in corporate and capital markets contexts where mandatory arbitration clauses bind dispersed investors — but have not yet produced systemic strain. Three conclusions follow. First, aggregation pressures can arise even where doctrinal foundations remain stable, as prevailing doctrine displaces rather than accommodates collective claims. Second, while arbitral institutions can mitigate coordination and capacity problems through procedural design, questions of representation and the binding effects of arbitral awards turn on issues of authority that institutional practice alone cannot resolve. Third, in a pre-crisis setting such as Brazil’s, these limits create an opportunity for institutional planning, allowing responses to scale to be considered in advance rather than improvised under stress.

title: Impact of Digital Finance Apps on the Financial Behaviour of Urban Millennials in India: A Pilot Study
affiliations: and

detail.title: Impact of Digital Finance Apps on the Financial Behaviour of Urban Millennials in India: A Pilot Study
detail.abstract: Digital finance applications (DFAs) have drastically altered how urban Indians manage their money. Yet, while adoption metrics are widely tracked, the specific psychological and behavioral outcomes of this technology remain under-researched. Grounded in the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT2) and Mental Accounting Theory, this pilot study (N=50) explores how DFA features and perceived trust shape the saving, spending, and investment habits of millennials (aged 25-40). Our primary objective is to validate a conceptual measurement model for future Structural Equation Modelling (SEM). Data, gathered via a 5-point Likert instrument, showed robust internal reliability (Cronbach's $\alpha$ = 0.93). The findings indicate SBI Yono is the preferred platform, closely followed by PhonePe. Crucially, correlation analysis confirms that higher app engagement is linked to both increased savings rates ($r = 0.62$) and higher discretionary spending ($r = 0.47$). This dichotomy suggests that while automated app features act as effective behavioral nudges for saving, frictionless payment interfaces simultaneously reduce the psychological "pain of paying." Ultimately, this pilot successfully validates the measurement instrument and establishes a strong theoretical baseline for large-scale SEM research.

title: Training need analysis of Veterinary Surgeons for animal healthcare sustainability: Capacity building and public health implications
affiliations: ,  and

detail.title: Training need analysis of Veterinary Surgeons for animal healthcare sustainability: Capacity building and public health implications
detail.abstract: The rapidly growing livestock health concern in India has increased the demand for skilled veterinary professionals capable of addressing clinical emergencies, emerging infectious diseases and technology-driven service delivery. Despite of an important role of veterinary surgeons in disease control and public health programs, very limited literature exists on competency gaps and training needs among government-employed veterinary surgeons in Haryana. This study was undertaken to (i) assess perceived training needs in six major competency areas, (ii) identify high-priority subareas requiring immediate capacity strengthening, and (iii) examine demographic determinants associated with training needs. A total of 286 veterinary surgeons working in government veterinary hospitals across Haryana were surveyed using a structured questionnaire covering 36 subareas of competencies under clinical, diagnostic, epidemiological and public health, ICT, soft skills and sustainability domains. Data were analyzed by using SPSS, 20th version software as per Snedecor and Cochran (1994). The results revealed consistently high training needs across all domains (mean: 3.93–4.35), with clinical (4.35 ±0.59) and diagnostic competencies (4.26 ±0.62) ranking highest. The top subareas include emergency and critical care (4.68), advanced diagnostics (PCR/ELISA) (4.59), dystocia management (4.48), outbreak investigation (4.43), and antimicrobial resistance stewardship (4.39). The negative correlation was found between training need and both age (r = –0.42) and experience (r = –0.47), signifying higher needs among early-career veterinarians. These findings provide actionable insights for practitioners seeking targeted capacity building and policymakers designing state-level continuing veterinary education (CVE), one health programs, and digital livestock health initiatives. Prioritizing evidence-based training modules will significantly strengthen Haryana's veterinary service delivery and disease preparedness capabilities.

title: Remote Work and Urban Sprawl
affiliations: and French Expertise and Study Center for Risks, Environment, Mobility and Planning (CEREMA)

detail.title: Remote Work and Urban Sprawl
detail.abstract: The Covid-19 pandemic has led to widespread remote work. Can land transfers from the workplace to residential areas help contain urban sprawl? Remote work can also take place in coworking spaces. We use a standard urban economics model to assess urban sprawl containment in the remote work era. We compare two scenarios: Working from home (WFH) and in coworking spaces. We show that remote work in coworking spaces leads to city expansion, while WFH causes city shrinkage. City size and household satisfaction are positively related. However, WFH can contain urban sprawl while maintaining satisfaction by carefully choosing remote work shares.

title: Understanding the Favorite–Longshot Bias: Review of Explanations and a Hedging-Based Mechanism

detail.title: Understanding the Favorite–Longshot Bias: Review of Explanations and a Hedging-Based Mechanism
detail.abstract: The Favorite-Longshot Bias (FLB) is one of the most persistent and well-documented anomalies in wagering markets, observed across multiple sports over the past 70 years. While prior research has attributed the bias to behavioral factors such as misperceptions of probability and risk-seeking tendencies, these explanations alone cannot fully account for its persistence. This paper provides a comprehensive review of the literature on the FLB, categorizing existing explanations into behavioral, informational, and structural mechanisms. Building on this review, we propose a novel explanation: the bias may emerge from bookmakers’ hedging practices. Specifically, risk management by bookmakers can systematically reduce the expected return on low-probability, high-value outcomes, generating a longshot bias even when bettors’ predictions are unbiased. We discuss empirical strategies to test the theory. Our findings contribute to a deeper understanding of market anomalies, the interaction between human behavior and institutional structures, and the role of risk management in shaping observed market biases.

title: Do EU Food Safety Inspections Follow the Harvest? Testing for Seasonal Protectionism in Border Rejections
affiliations: Universidade Federal de Viçosa (UFV), FEA-USP and Universidade Federal de Viçosa (UFV)

detail.title: Do EU Food Safety Inspections Follow the Harvest? Testing for Seasonal Protectionism in Border Rejections

declarations.ethicsApproval: None
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: Whether sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) enforcement serves as disguised protectionism is a long-standing concern in agricultural trade policy. This paper tests whether EU member states reject more imported food at the border during the domestic harvest season of the same product. We construct a panel of 2.5 million observations integrating border rejection records from the Rapid Alert System for Food and Feed (RASFF), bilateral trade flows from COMEXT, and member state-level harvest calendars from Eurostat production data (2008-2025). A linear probability model with high-dimensional fixed effects identifies the harvest effect from withincorridor, within-year variation. The results do not support seasonal protectionism: the harvest coefficient is indistinguishable from zero across specifications, the placebo with non-EUcultivated products passes, and temporal leads show no effect. A power analysis confirms that the test would detect effects as small as 0.045 percentage points (22.5% of baseline). What does predict rejections is past non-compliance: the 3-month rejection lag raises the probability by 2.04 percentage points, more than ten times the baseline. Decomposing cross-product spillovers by hazard type suggests that compliance-related rejections (labelling, documentation) generate positive spillover to other products from the same origin, while contaminant-related rejections do not, though this result is estimated from a limited number of observations. These findings reframe the policy challenge: the obstacle to EU market access for developing-country food exporters is not the timing of inspections but a self-reinforcing reputational cycle that penalizes countries with weak compliance infrastructure.

title: A Mechanism for Addressing Participation and Compliance for the Provision of Global Public Goods
affiliations: University of Graz, University of Kiel and Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research (PIK)

detail.title: A Mechanism for Addressing Participation and Compliance for the Provision of Global Public Goods
detail.abstract: In a three-stage global public good coalition formation game, Kornek and Edenhofer (2020) propose a transfer scheme in the spirit of mechanism design which allows to stabilize large coalitions, including the grand coalition. The transfer scheme addresses the free-rider problem in terms of participation. In order to address the free-rider problem in terms of compliance with transfer obligations, they propose a deposit-refund scheme in the spirit of Gerber and Wichardt (2009) and others. However, McEvoy and McGinty (2023) argue in a comment that the compliance issue has not yet been solved because signatories would have neither an incentive to pay the deposit nor the transfer. Therefore, in this paper, we divide the entire game into four stages and demonstrate in detail that compliance is an equilibrium strategy for each decision in the game. Subsequently, we argue that the game can be simplified by merging stages. We also demonstrate that the transfer scheme retains its desirable properties by considering asymmetric countries. It emerges that it is promising to generalize further the setting of Kornek and Edenhofer (2020).

title: Risk, Time, and Diet Quality:  Evidence from a General Population Survey
affiliations: University Paris-Saclay, INRAE, AgroParisTech, Paris-Saclay Applied Economics, Université Paris X Nanterre, HEC Paris and University Paris-Saclay, INRAE, AgroParisTech, Paris-Saclay Applied Economics

detail.title: Risk, Time, and Diet Quality:  Evidence from a General Population Survey
detail.abstract: This paper explores the relationships between overall diet quality and attitudes toward risk and time using a general population survey. We combine a state-of-the-art food frequency questionnaire and a choice-based preference module to elicit individual risk and time preferences. The online questionnaire was administered to a socioeconomic panel representative of the French population. We show that risk and time preferences are associated with individual heterogeneity in key aspects of diet quality, a result that holds across a wide range of robustness checks.Using a hierarchical Bayes framework, we jointly estimate individual risk aversion and impatience parameters and show that associations hold for both model-free and structural estimates of risk and time preferences.We further show that these associations account for a substantial share of the heterogeneity in dietary outcomes beyond sociodemographic controls.However, despite their importance for individual heterogeneity, behavioral preferences explain little of the observed socioeconomic gradients in diet quality.

title: Green Public Procurement: International Evidence
affiliations: , University of Toronto - Rotman School of Management, University of Waterloo and

detail.title: Green Public Procurement: International Evidence
detail.abstract: Markets often fail to generate sufficient incentives for corporations to invest in environmentally responsible practices at socially optimal levels. Green public procurement has emerged as a key policy tool for encouraging government suppliers to adopt green innovations. This study presents a large-scale, multi-country analysis of supplier firms engaged in green procurement contracts, examining their characteristics and environmental outcomes. In our determinant analyses, we find that politically connected firms, those with higher CO2 emissions, and firms with prior procurement experience are more likely to secure green contracts (and obtain higher-value contracts). Cross-sectional analyses corroborate our findings and indicate predictable heterogeneity in in how these factors affect green contract allocation. In our consequences analyses, we show that participation in such contracts is associated with subsequent CO2 reductions, some improvement in product sustainability awareness, and greater disengagement from non-compliant suppliers. A difference-indifferences analysis corroborates these findings. Overall, the evidence highlights green procurement contracts as an effective environmental policy instrument for advancing sustainable development, with important socioeconomic relevance and clear policy implications.

title: Wedded to the State: Elite Social Networks and Territorial Integration in Early Modern Venice
affiliations: and

detail.title: Wedded to the State: Elite Social Networks and Territorial Integration in Early Modern Venice
detail.abstract: We examine how states integrate peripheral elites by overcoming credible commitment problems that weaken taxation, public debt, and security provision. We argue that elite marriage networks can serve as an "exchange of hostages," binding central and peripheral elites through kinship ties that raise the costs of ex post opportunism and render fiscal and security promises credible. We test this mechanism in early modern Venice, where the 1630 plague and the fiscal demands of the War of Crete induced a previously closed nobility to admit wealthy mainland families. Using newly digitized family-level data on marriages, offices, and public debt holdings, we show that families integrated earlier into the noble marriage network were more likely to invest in public debt than later entrants. Integration is also associated with higher provincial tax revenues, increased military spending, and a stronger central institutional presence. These findings highlight the relational foundations of state territorial integration.

title: When DEI Policies Discriminate Against DEI Candidates
affiliations: Indian School of Business, University of Michigan, Stephen M. Ross School of Business and Indian School of Business

detail.title: When DEI Policies Discriminate Against DEI Candidates
detail.abstract: This study shows that a firm's DEI employee policy can favor a DEI job candidate in partial equilibrium, but can hurt her in general equilibrium. The reason is that DEI policies are often opaque and so a firm that would otherwise have been the correct match for a DEI candidate purely on a merit basis may believe that she may land an even better offer on DEI grounds. The firm may thus pass on her and settle for an inferior but sure non-DEI candidate. This behavior could cascade across firms, and eventually end up leaving the DEI candidate jobless, which would have never happened to her in a pure merit-based job market. Our model suggests that the empirically documented failure of DEI policies to benefit DEI candidates may be a general equilibrium artifact that is no firm's fault, and not willful diversity washing or tokenism by firms, as has been suggested in prior empirical accounting research.

title: Changing Modes or Changing Pollsters? U.S. Presidential Election Polls From 2016 to 2024
affiliations: University of Montreal

detail.title: Changing Modes or Changing Pollsters? U.S. Presidential Election Polls From 2016 to 2024

declarations.ethicsApproval: No ethics approval necessary, no research on human beings
declarations.funderStatement: This research has not been funded.

detail.abstract:
U.S. presidential election polling has been intensely scrutinized since 2016, when national polls correctly estimated the popular vote but failed to predict the Electoral College winner, creating a widespread perception of polling failure. Subsequent publications nonetheless emphasized that the pollsters had improved their methods for the next election and, specifically, adopted adjustments for education. However, less attention has been paid to the structural changes in the polling industry, particularly shifts in the modes of administration. This article examines all publicly released polls conducted between September 1 and Election Day in the 2016, 2020, and 2024 U.S. presidential elections to determine whether methodological adaptation within firms occurred or whether there were transformations in the composition of the polling field. Drawing on data compiled from public sources and validated through multiple platforms, this study tracked 80 polling organizations that conducted at least one poll in at least one of the elections. They were categorized by mode of administration (live phone, web, or mixed). 

The results show that the variation in mode usage across elections was driven less by pollsters refining their methods than by high entry and exit rates. Only 20% of pollsters changed their mode over time, while more than half appeared in only one election. The surge of web-based pollsters in 2020—an election marked by the largest polling error since 1980—was partly due to new entrants, many of whom underestimated the Republican vote. Mixed-mode pollsters performed better in 2016 and 2020, helping to explain their growth by 2024. By 2024, the differences in performance across modes had largely disappeared, and polls accurately estimated both vote shares and the winner.

The good news is that this instability in the polling field did not significantly affect the quality of the estimates, except marginally in 2020. However, greater transparency and stronger professional standards would help better understand whether other pollsters’ practices could explain polling misses and failures.

title: Limited Climate Change Adaptation Capacity of the European Nature Restoration Regulation
affiliations: University Grenoble Alpes, University Grenoble Alpes, University Grenoble Alpes and University Grenoble Alpes

detail.title: Limited Climate Change Adaptation Capacity of the European Nature Restoration Regulation
detail.abstract: The European Nature Restoration Regulation (NRR) aims to scale Nature-based Solutions across ecosystems in Europe. We evaluate its potential across the Alps for delivering ecosystem services and climate change adaptation for three of its binding targets: i) restoring rivers; ii) increasing urban green spaces in cities; and iii) integrating hedgerows into agricultural landscapes. Our analysis indicates the potential of implementing the regulation to mitigate floods from rivers. However, the capacity of the NRR to mitigate heatwaves in urban areas is limited, and we found no significant effect of hedgerow implementation for drought adaptation through groundwater recharge in agricultural landscapes. Our spatially explicit cost-benefit analysis demonstrates that the NRR would be more cost-effective if vulnerable areas were prioritized. Overall, these findings call for an increase of the ambition and budget of the NRR to effectively address climate change adaptation.

title: A Qualitative Study On Cultivating Customer Loyalty In Cross-Border E-Commerce
affiliations: UPM

detail.title: A Qualitative Study On Cultivating Customer Loyalty In Cross-Border E-Commerce
detail.abstract: The rapid growth of cross-border e-commerce presents significant challenges in maintaining customer loyalty due to issues of trust, logistical complexities, cultural differences, and service quality. While existing literature offers substantial quantitative insights into the factors influencing loyalty, a deep, narrative understanding of the customer experience remains underexplored. This qualitative study aims to address this gap by investigating the lived experiences, emotions, and perceptions of cross-border shoppers. Employing an interpretive, phenomenological approach, data was collected through in-depth, semi-structured interviews and focus group discussions with regular cross-border e-commerce consumers. Thematic analysis was used to analyze the data. The findings reveal that trust is not merely a factor but a complex process built through transparency, communication, and post-purchase support. Emotional connections, shaped by positive service recovery and personalized interactions, play a crucial role in fostering loyalty beyond satisfaction. Furthermore, perceptions of brand image and service quality are deeply intertwined with cultural compatibility and reliable fulfillment promises. The study concludes that cultivating loyalty in cross-border e-commerce requires a holistic strategy that addresses the emotional and experiential dimensions of the customer journey. Theoretical contributions include enriching the application of relationship marketing and trust theories in digital, cross-cultural contexts. Practical implications provide online retailers with actionable insights for improving customer experience, designing effective communication, and building sustainable loyalty programs.

title: Will Central Clearing Change the Market Structure of U.S. Treasury Repo to Become More Standardized and Trade on an All-to-All Basis?
affiliations: Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago

detail.title: Will Central Clearing Change the Market Structure of U.S. Treasury Repo to Become More Standardized and Trade on an All-to-All Basis?

publicationDetails.detailsText: FRB of Chicago Working Paper No. 2026-02
publicationDetails.journalName: Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper examines whether the SEC's mandate for central clearing of U.S. Treasury repo transactions could enable all-to-all trading and support the development of a standardized term repo market. By mitigating counterparty risk through central clearing, cash lenders may become more willing to transact directly with a broader set of borrowers, reducing reliance on dealer intermediation. Clearing may also encourage greater participation in term repos beyond overnight tenors if counterparty risk is reduced. However, for all-to-all trading to take hold, the market must adopt more standardized contract terms, collateral schedules, and operational protocols such as consolidated trade execution and post-trade processing. If these structural and operational hurdles are addressed, an all-to-all term repo market could emerge-enhancing liquidity, reducing rollover risk, and improving the resilience of the U.S. financial system.

title: Why Science Needs Causal Problem Modelling
affiliations: Anglia Ruskin University

detail.title: Why Science Needs Causal Problem Modelling
detail.abstract:
Science now operates in an era of unprecedented data, computational power, and AI (artificial intelligence)-driven ideation, yet scientific inquiry seemingly remains largely fragmented across disciplinary boundaries. Econometrics, machine learning, nonlinear dynamics, evolutionary economics, sociology, psychology, political science, and AI engineering all study causal processes, but each relies on distinct conceptual vocabularies, representational logics, and methodological assumptions. This fragmentation can limit the capacity of researchers and policymakers to communicate, to integrate evidence, and to design effective interventions in complex adaptive systems. 

We argue that contemporary science lacks a unifying upstream discipline that takes the causal problem itself, rather than data, statistical tools, or domain-specific models, as the primary unit of analysis. We introduce Causal Problem Modelling (CPM) as this missing discipline. CPM formalises what researchers implicitly construct but rarely articulate, the causal architecture, the feasible intervention set, the data-generating situation, the identification surface, and the counterfactual constraint set. These primitives provide a domain-general language for representing causal systems that can be applied uniformly across the natural and social sciences. 

CPM extends the Sussex lineage of innovation studies, evolutionary economics, sectoral systems, and institutional theory by giving these traditions a formal causal structure they historically lacked. It also unifies insights from nonlinear dynamics, behavioural science, interpretive social science, and metascience, clarifying where different methods contribute and where identification is inherently limited. By distinguishing what CPM is, and is not, the framework avoids conflation with potential outcomes, structural causal models, econometric identification strategies, machine learning, and complexity models, positioning CPM as an upstream integrative discipline rather than a competing methodology. 

CPM also provides a principled foundation for AI integration in science and policy. Treating AI systems as structural instruments for architecture discovery, dynamic simulation, and counterfactual exploration, CPM enables responsible, transparent, and ethically bounded use of AI in high-stakes domains. We illustrate how CPM can guide intervention design, policy evaluation, and scientific governance in systems characterised by feedback, emergence, heterogeneity, uncertainty, and institutional constraints. 

In establishing CPM as a field in its own right, this article offers a coherent framework for designing interventions, integrating heterogeneous evidence, coordinating interdisciplinary teams, and governing complex socio-technical systems. CPM provides a foundation for the next phase of scientific practice, a unifying discipline for understanding and shaping the causal systems that define the modern world.

title: Exploring Success Variables of Knowledge Management for Enhanced Organisational Performance: An Integrated Framework

detail.title: Exploring Success Variables of Knowledge Management for Enhanced Organisational Performance: An Integrated Framework

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No potential conflict of interest was reported by the author.
declarations.ethicsApproval: The author does not analyse or generate any datasets, because this is a conceptual paper, which proceeds within a literature survey approach.
declarations.funderStatement: Part of this work was supported by the University Grants Commission of Bangladesh (2014-0862/001-001) and administered by Begum Rokeya University, Rangpur.

detail.abstract: Knowledge management (KM) plays a pivotal role in the dynamic landscape of contemporary organisations. Effectively managing vital knowledge resources is a primary concern for decision makers, necessitating comprehensive consideration of pertinent variables for KM success. This study seeks to identify KM success variables (SVs) and their impact on organisational performance (OP) intervening through mediating variables (MVs). Then it aims to develop an integrated framework based on the scrutinised variables. To accomplish the intended objective, the author employs a systematic literature review (SLR) technique. From 57 chosen studies, 34 KM-SVs are identified that have impacts on OP through three kinds of MVs. These SVs are categorised into nine divisions: infrastructure-oriented, organisation-wide, management-related, practice-oriented, skills-based, resource-based, KM-centred, network-based and supporting variables. Basing upon these variables, an integrated conceptual framework is developed. The findings hold practical utility for knowledge-intensive organisations and decision makers as well as it proposes avenues for future research in this realm.

title: Managing Retirement Risk: Policy Choices in Pension Fund Administration
affiliations: Independent and Bowen University Iwo, Nigeria

detail.title: Managing Retirement Risk: Policy Choices in Pension Fund Administration
detail.abstract:
This article critically examines the legal and institutional framework governing pension administration and Pension Fund Administrators in Nigeria under the Pension Reform Act 2014. It analyses the structure of the contributory pension scheme, focusing on the statutory separation between Pension Fund Administrators and Pension Fund Custodians as well as the fiduciary obligations imposed on administrators, and the supervisory mandate of the National Pension Commission. The study situates Nigeria's pension reforms within the broader global shift from unfunded public schemes to regulated, privately managed contributory systems. 

Adopting a doctrinal and comparative policy methodology, the article evaluates Nigeria's regulatory framework alongside selected frontier markets like India, Singapore and South Africa with similar reform trajectories. The comparison considers a various number of factors including, but not limited to; governance standards, supervisory approaches, investment regulation, and mechanisms for risk control and contributor protection. While Nigeria's framework demonstrates important structural safeguards and significant asset growth, gaps remain, particularly within the informal sector. 

The article argues that strengthening risk based supervision is necessary to consolidate public trust and ensure the long term sustainability of Nigeria's pension system.

title: Generative AI and the Reallocation of Time: Productivity, Leisure, and Fulfilling Work
affiliations: and The Bank of Korea

detail.title: Generative AI and the Reallocation of Time: Productivity, Leisure, and Fulfilling Work

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The survey conducted in the paper was funded by the Bank of Korea.
declarations.funderStatement: The survey conducted in the paper was funded by the Bank of Korea.

detail.abstract: Using a representative survey of Korean workers, we provide evidence on the adoption of Generative AI (GenAI) and how GenAI reallocates time at work. We find that 51.8% of workers use GenAI for work and GenAI reduces working time by 3.8%. However, these gains may not materialize in aggregate productivity statistics yet: the correlation between time savings and output changes is near zero. We show this disconnect arises because workers capture efficiency gains primarily as on-the-job leisure, rather than increasing their output. These findings suggest that standard productivity measures may understate AI's impact by missing non-pecuniary welfare channels.

title: Should We take Trump’s Board of Peace Literally — or Seriously?
affiliations: National University of Singapore (NUS) - Faculty of Law

detail.title: Should We take Trump’s Board of Peace Literally — or Seriously?
detail.abstract:
The inauguration of President Donald Trump’s Board of Peace marks a notable development in contemporary international institutional design. Initially welcomed by the United Nations Security Council in Resolution 2803 (2025) as a transitional mechanism related to Gaza, the Board was subsequently launched at Davos as a self-described international organization with a broader global mandate. This article examines the Board’s Charter and governance structure, arguing that while formally corporate in legal design, it concentrates authority in an unusually personalised executive role. The analysis situates the Board within longer traditions of international ordering — contrasting liberal institutionalism and realism with what may be described as a form of “neo-royalism,” in which legitimacy is grounded in hierarchical leadership and effectiveness rather than sovereign equality and procedural constraint.

Rather than dismissing the Board as aberrational, the article interprets it as symptomatic of wider dissatisfaction with established multilateral institutions. Drawing parallels between domestic populist critiques of institutional liberalism and emerging experimentation in international governance, it asks whether the Board represents a durable alternative to UN-centred multilateralism or another episode in a recurring pattern of ad hoc institutional innovation. The article concludes by considering the implications for small and medium-sized states that must navigate between principled commitment to a rules-based order and pragmatic engagement with evolving power structures.

title: Local Fiscal Consequences of State Sports-Betting Tax Policy
affiliations: University of Iowa - Department of Finance and University of Alabama - Culverhouse College of Commerce & Business Administration

detail.title: Local Fiscal Consequences of State Sports-Betting Tax Policy
detail.abstract: Thirty-eight states have legalized sports betting since 2018, yet policy debates ignore local governments. We ask whether state sports betting policy affects local fiscal health. Using municipal bond yields (2018-2024) and Census of Governments data (2017-2022), we estimate an imputation difference-indifferences model exploiting staggered legalization and cross-sectional variation in tax rates. Legalization improves local fiscal conditions, but higher state tax rates diminish these gains. Across all legalizing states, bond yields fall by approximately 10 basis points and municipal sales tax revenue rises by roughly $44,000 per municipality. At the median tax rate (15%), the yield reduction is approximately 14 basis points and the revenue gain is roughly $36,000. Each percentage point increase in the state tax rate erodes these benefits. We find no extensive-margin effect on intergovernmental transfers, suggesting effects flow through consumer spending rather than revenue-sharing.

title: Emerging Innovation but Little Systematic Progress: Social Dialogue on Artificial Intelligence in France
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Emerging Innovation but Little Systematic Progress: Social Dialogue on Artificial Intelligence in France

publicationDetails.detailsText: Rainone S. and Zwyzen W. (eds.) Collective Bargaining in the Age of AI – Vol. 1: Country Evidence and EU Perspectives, ETUI

detail.abstract:
This chapter examines the development of social dialogue on artificial intelligence (AI) in France. While public authorities and social partners increasingly frame social dialogue as a key tool to co-construct AI uses and regulate risks, actual progress remains uneven. Although official statistics suggest limited diffusion, employee surveys reveal widespread and often undeclared “shadow AI” use, especially since the rise of generative AI.

French labour law already provides significant levers—through information and consultation rights on new technologies, training obligations, health and safety duties, collective bargaining. Recent court rulings have reinforced information and consultation rights, including during pilot phases. However, collective agreements explicitly addressing AI remain rare and often treat it indirectly, embedding AI-related issues within traditional bargaining topics such as data protection, skills, or non-discrimination rather than creating specific rights on algorithmic management.

A few innovative agreements introduce iterative forms of technological social dialogue, involving worker representatives early and throughout the AI lifecycle. The Dial-IA project exemplifies this approach. Overall, the French case shows emerging experimentation but still limited systematic institutionalisation.

title: A Simulation-based Approach to Asset Allocation for Sovereign Funds
affiliations: Allocation Strategy Ltd. and Allocation Strategy Ltd.

detail.title: A Simulation-based Approach to Asset Allocation for Sovereign Funds
detail.abstract: We develop a simulation-based framework for analysing asset allocation decisions alongside key economic drivers for sovereign funds. Together with realistic asset prices connected to macro, we model fiscal deficits, commodity revenues, exchange rates, gold reserves, and sovereign debt. By integrating these components within a consistent macro-financial structure, the model captures important interactions that shape long-horizon risks for public funds. The model provides a quantitative framework for evaluating trade-offs inherent in asset allocation decisions. We provide a stylised example where gold reserves are converted into a multi-asset portfolio, and show how these different portfolios interact with macro outcomes.

title: Consumption Upgrading and Wage Inequality

detail.title: Consumption Upgrading and Wage Inequality
detail.abstract: This paper examines how long-run economic growth shapes wage inequality through the joint evolution of household preferences and production technologies. I develop a unified framework that combines capital-skill complementarity with demand-side forces arising from nonhomothetic consumption behavior. Using household expenditure data linked to detailed occupation-industry information, I document two key empirical facts: (i) in the cross-section, richer households allocate a larger share of their spending to goods and services that are more skill-intensive to produce, and (ii) over time, households have increasingly shifted their expenditures toward high-skillintensive goods over time. These patterns are consistent with prior work that has used more aggregated data. While the first suggests the potential importance of technological growth, the second fact points to nonhomothetic demand. To disentangle and quantify these two forces, I construct a multi-industry general equilibrium model featuring nonhomothetic demand, industry-specific technologies, and capital-skill complementarity. The model explains the rise in the U.S. skill premium between 1982 and 2019 through three mechanisms: an income-driven demand shift toward high-skill goods (accounting for about 5 percent of the increase), capital accumulation interacting with capital-skill complementarity (about 82 percent), and faster productivity growth in skill-intensive industries that lowers their relative prices and further amplifies demand (roughly 10 percent).

detail.abstract: This paper studies capital misallocation in a tractable model with random fixed costs of adjustment. We identify the distribution of fixed costs and productivity shocks using the entire size distribution and frequency of investments and provide an efficient estimation method. We derive the measure of capital misallocation in the presence of fixed costs and show that it differs from the traditional metric based on the variance of marginal product of capital. The key feature of models with lumpy investments responsible for this is their non-linearity: the distribution of marginal product of capital is not log-normal even with normal shocks and non-degenerate even when shocks are small. We apply our method to 40 years of panel data on Italian firms and find misallocation costs about 0.5-2% of output. Fixed costs contribute about one half to traditional measures of TFPR dispersion, putting an upper bound on potential inefficiencies.

title: Inaccurate Beliefs and Cyclical Labor Market Dynamics

detail.title: Inaccurate Beliefs and Cyclical Labor Market Dynamics
detail.abstract: This paper examines how systematic biases and heterogeneity in beliefs about the state of the economy shape wage dynamics, labor market flows, and aggregate responses to shocks. I present survey evidence that households form dispersed, backwardlooking expectations about macroeconomic conditions, with more optimistic workers demanding higher wages. Motivated by these findings, I develop a search-and-matching model with sticky wages and endogenous separations where workers and firms face information frictions about the aggregate state of the economy. The model is disciplined using data from the Michigan Survey of Consumers and Survey of Professional Forecasters, targeting key empirical moments. In equilibrium, the gap between firm and worker beliefs drives unemployment volatility, while firm learning raises the persistence of the economy's response to shocks but dampens volatility. Allowing for heterogeneity in workers' learning rates explains observed differences in employment transitions: Workers with more sluggish beliefs remain overly optimistic in recessions, are hired at higher wages, and face a higher risk of separation.
