detail.abstract: After a period of moderating cost increases, businesses faced mounting cost pressures in 2025. While tariffs played a role in driving up the costs of many inputs—especially among manufacturers—they represent only part of the story. Indeed, firms grappled with substantial cost increases across many categories in the past year. This post is the first in a three-part series analyzing cost and price dynamics among businesses in the New York-Northern New Jersey region based on data collected through our regional business surveys. Firms reported that the sharpest cost increases over the past year were for employee health insurance and utilities, followed by business insurance, and goods and materials inputs. Firms expect cost growth to moderate in 2026. Our second post will examine the sharp increase in employee health insurance costs in more detail and show that such rising costs dampened wage growth for some workers. The third post will analyze firms’ pricing behavior in light of these cost pressures, as well as firms’ inflation expectations.

detail.abstract: Using electric vehicles (EVs) as power storage is referred to as vehicleto-grid (V2G). With V2G, the EV may serve two needs: transportation and when parked, electricity market stabilization, which will become increasingly important as the share of intermittent renewable power in the power mix grows. To our knowledge no study has yet analyzed how V2G interacts with intermittent renewables. In this paper we ask: i) Do V2G and intermittent renewables mutually benefit each other, and if so: ii) Should V2G be subsidized? We show analytically that increasing the share of EV owners with V2G lowers the expected price of electricity. Nevertheless, investments in renewable energy are spurred as their production weighted price increases. Electricity consumers with inelastic demand will be better off, while baseload and price-responsive electricity producers will tend to be worse off with V2G. Moreover, we show that the laissez faire market uptake of V2G is efficient, and hence no subsidies are warranted. Finally, we calibrate the model to the German electricity market in 2035 and provide some illustrative, quantitative results. Among others we find that socially efficient adoption of V2G will increase electricity production from renewables by nearly 2 percent due to higher investments. Results also indicate that there could be a positive terms of trade effect for Germany of V2G implementation.

Employer-sponsored health insurance represents a substantial component of total compensation paid by firms to many workers in the United States. Such costs have climbed by close to 20 percent over the past five years. Our February regional business surveys asked firms whether their wage setting decisions were influenced by the rising cost of employee health insurance. As we showed in our companion post, respondents reported an average increase in such costs of more than 13 percent this year. Businesses providing insurance to their workers indicated that absent these cost increases, they would have raised wages by roughly an additional percentage point, on average, suggesting that rising health insurance costs resulted in a drag on wage growth for workers at these firms.

detail.abstract: In recent years, a growing number of countries have enacted tax rules that require multinational enterprises (MNEs) to document their intra-firm trade prices and show that they are set as in third-party trade. The objective of these rules is to limit opportunities for strategic trade mis-pricing and profit shifting to lower-tax affiliates. In this paper, we study the regulations' fiscal and real effects. detail.abstract:
Businesses experienced substantial cost pressures in 2025 as the cost of insurance and utilities rose sharply, while an increase in tariffs contributed to rising goods and materials costs. This post examines how firms in the New York-Northern New Jersey region adjusted their prices in response to these cost pressures and describes their expectations for future price increases and inflation. Survey results show an acceleration in firms’ price increases in 2025, with an especially sharp increase in the manufacturing sector. While both cost and price increases intensified last year, our surveys reveal that these do not contribute to firms believing that inflation will be on the rise in the short or longer term. In fact, firms’ inflation expectations have moderated compared to what was expected a year ago. Firms now anticipate inflation of 3 percent in the year ahead, lower than what was expected last year at this time. Importantly, like last year, longer-term inflation expectations also remain well anchored.

detail.abstract: This paper examines global labor outsourcing as a contemporary form of economic violence through which harm is externalized, obscured, and rendered morally distant. It argues that in 2025, the United States and other advanced democracies increasingly sustain domestic prosperity by exporting precarity, exploitation, and environmental harm through global supply chains that fragment responsibility while preserving legality. Drawing on international human rights law, global political economy, and moral philosophy, the analysis shows how legal neutrality, corporate impunity, and voluntary compliance regimes enable states and consumers to benefit from injustice without direct coercion or visible wrongdoing. Workers in the Global South-particularly women, children, and migrant laborers-are governed as expendable populations whose suffering is normalized through distance, abstraction, and market logic. By treating global labor systems as sites of governance rather than neutral markets, the paper contends that outsourcing functions as a moral technology that reallocates risk downward and outward, allowing democracies to evade ethical responsibility. It concludes that injustice cannot be exported without consequence: when prosperity depends on invisible harm, democratic legitimacy itself is placed at risk. Publication Note This paper is part of an independent research series examining moral drift, structural violence, and ethical failure in contemporary governance and global political economy. Extending earlier analyses of war, discrimination, and domestic social sorting, it shifts the focus beyond national borders to examine how harm is externalized through global labor systems and supply chains. Adopting an international, non-U.S. perspective grounded in human rights and moral philosophy, the paper treats outsourcing not as a neutral market process but as a moral and political structure that redistributes risk, suffering, and disposability across populations. The paper functions both as a standalone scholarly contribution and as a sequential chapter within a larger book-length manuscript on power and moral responsibility in 2025.

detail.abstract:
This paper introduces two simple modifications to the standard two-country open macroeconomic model with nominal bonds traded internationally: (i) both country-specific and global asset markets are incomplete, and (ii) acquiring foreign assets involves a transaction cost. We show that these departures from the benchmark model are sufficient to address the challenge posed by Lustig and Verdelhan (2019), who highlight three empirical facts about exchange rates-high volatility (standard deviation of 11%), a sizable currency risk premium, and near-zero cyclicality-and argue that the standard model fails to match them. Moreover, reconciling the high equity Sharpe ratio with a volatile stochastic discount factor (SDF) is also difficult in the baseline framework. 
We further relate our results to Chernov et al. (2023), who propose the need for international arbitrageurs to account for exchange rate dynamics, emphasizing that a large portion of exchange rate variation is unspanned by financial markets. In contrast, our model-with a simple asset structure and no international arbitrageurs-can account for the key empirical features they emphasize. 
Modest deviations from standard assumptions can go a long way in accounting for exchange rate behavior. This suggests that even simple financial market frictions can significantly enhance our understanding of exchange rates-perhaps more than previously believed by some.

detail.abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic had devastating global and domestic economic and health impacts. While these effects are broadly understood, the impact of COVID-19 on the Mongolian mining sector, a key economic sector, remains unclear. This study seeks to bridge this knowledge gap by analyzing relevant secondary data, conducting a survey of mining companies, and simulating near-term economic outlooks using a recursive dynamic CGE model. The study concluded that the slowdown of the Mongolian mining sector was a driving force behind the overall economic slowdown during the COVID-19 pandemic. The mining sector was affected by various external and internal shocks, including fluctuations in Chinese demand, price shocks, and COVID-19 related government restrictions. Most surveyed mining companies reported decreases in both sales and production, coupled with numerous labor, production, and transportation issues arising from COVID-19 related restrictions. While differences existed across commodities, most mining companies were optimistic about future recovery. Given the study's finding that the post-COVID-19 economic recovery will be closely linked to the mining sector's recovery, we simulated 3 alternative mining-sector recovery scenarios using an in-house CGE model. Overall, the simulation results highlighted the detrimental economic effect of continued pandemic conditions and the need to diversify the Mongolian economy beyond mining. In light of these findings, the government must balance the consequences of COVID-19-related measures for the mining sector with the need to contain the pandemic.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the persistence of educational inequalities in Africa, focusing on colonial and contemporary Congo. By analyzing historical and contemporary surveys, archives, and school administrative data, we document the continuing impact of colonial-era factors and explore mechanisms of path dependency. We find that contemporary educational inequalities are driven by the clustering of postindependence schools around historical Christian missions. This clustering dynamic has increased over time and is shaped by religious competition between schools of different denominations. This spatial pattern significantly affects girls' education more than boys' because girls are more sensitive to distance barriers, explaining a stronger colonial legacy for female education. Our analysis suggests that parental education and missions as agents of structural change have limited influence on regional educational outcomes in this context.

detail.abstract: We study an irreversible investment problem with endogenous scale under uncertainty, characterized by a concave subsidy schedule featuring a policy-induced kink. Using a real options framework, we analyze how the structure of policy support, in particular, the presence of threshold-induced kinks, reshapes optimal investment timing and scale. Motivated by the recent reform of the Common Agricultural Policy, which introduced redistributive payments linked to "first hectares", we show that nonsmooth support schemes fundamentally alter investment incentives. Smaller projects respond to higher subsidies by expanding investment scale without affecting timing, while larger projects exhibit non-monotonic responses: higher basic payments encourage expansion but delay investment, whereas stronger redistributive components induce earlier investment in smaller projects. These asymmetric responses generate a pooling effect around the policy threshold, whereby heterogeneous investors optimally converge to similar project sizes. By introducing policy-induced kinks into a real options model with endogenous scale, the analysis shows that redistributive subsidies can generate pooling and non-monotonic timing-scale responses that cannot arise under smooth or linear payoff structures. More generally, the results highlight how non-linear subsidies affect irreversible investment decisions, with implications for subsidy capitalization and the dynamic allocation of land.

detail.abstract: National innovation policies are designed to stimulate firm-level innovation; however, their micro-level impacts and underlying mechanisms differ across countries. This paper examines the impacts of China's Intellectual Property Pilot and Demonstration City (IPPDC) policy on firms' patenting behaviour, using unique handpicked firm-level patent and R&D data from 2008 to 2022. Employing a multi-period difference-indifference estimator (CSDID) on a propensityscore-matched sample of Chinese manufacturing firms, we find that the IPPDC policy program significantly enhances firm-level innovation, primarily through increased city-level investments in science, technology, and education, which in turn stimulate corporate R&D expenditure. Significant heterogeneity exists in different subgroups: positive impacts are pronounced among large firms, but for small firms, the effects are negative; firms in less competitive markets are more likely to increase innovation, and firms without separation of management and ownership are more likely to promote innovation activities. Regional differences also emerge with coastal firms only prioritising technological innovation, while inland firms also focus on non-technological patents. Our findings remain robust across various checks and reveal that the policy delivers both immediate and sustained long-term effects, underscoring its success in fostering innovation.

detail.abstract: Data on marriage flows are not available in most developing countries, making marriage market imbalance difficult to measure. Existing measures use crude fertility rates and do not account for early-life mortality, overstating the number of births surviving to marriageable ages. This paper develops the Surplus Groom Index to quantify marriage market imbalance under monogamy using census age structure, vital registration of births and deaths, and marriage timing data. The index incorporates effective fertility-total births adjusted for under-five mortality-to reflect actual cohort progression from birth to marriageable ages. This adjustment matters in settings where child mortality shapes the supply of marriage partners. Using India's 2011 Census data, we find that eleven percent of men aged 15-54 cannot marry due to bride shortage, approximately 39 million men. Marriage imbalance is widespread rather than regionally concentrated. Punjab records the highest deficit at 33 percent, but states considered demographically progressive show substantial imbalance: Kerala 18 percent, West Bengal 14 percent, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu 11 percent each. Declining fertility has produced smaller female cohorts unable to absorb male-heavy cohorts from earlier birth years. Balanced sex ratios at birth do not ensure marriage market equilibrium once fertility declines and marriage is delayed.

detail.abstract: Unrestricted mixed-data sampling (U-MIDAS) models are widely used to incorporate high-frequency data into forecasts of low-frequency macroeconomic outcomes, but they often become unstable when the frequency mismatch is large. Using a continuous-time embedding, we show that under extreme frequency mismatch, U-MIDAS attempts to recover more information than the data can support, leading to an ill-posed inverse problem for the lag-weight function. We propose smoothing-spline regularization as a practical solution that stabilizes estimation and allows researchers to make interpretable statements about when high-frequency information matters within a period-for example, through cumulative and late-quarter effects. A Bayesian implementation provides transparent uncertainty quantification for these timing summaries. Simulations and applications to US GDP nowcasting and macroeconomic uncertainty measurement show that the approach delivers stable estimates and economically meaningful inference in settings with dense high-frequency data. Overall, our results justify inference on economically interpretable within-period timing measures even when pointwise lag estimates are unreliable.

detail.abstract:
This article explores the need to regulate microtransactions in video games that may simulate gambling in-game content. The convergence of gambling and digital games is examined, particularly through the example of loot boxes as random items purchased for real money. Gambling is considered here as requiring state regulation, and its presence in video games without age restrictions may become a dangerous practice for consumers and encourage further involvement in such gambling in the future. In addition, virtual environments managed by technology companies may engage in exploitative policies towards users, encouraging addictive behaviour and selling in-game content in a deceptive manner through incomplete disclosure of information about possible winnings.

Thus, this work examined completely different models of regulation: European and Asian. The first of them, at the level of the European Union, leaves this issue to the consideration of the member states. For example, countries such as the United Kingdom and France have not yet assumed responsibility for state regulation of microtransactions in video games, and Belgium and the Netherlands have recognised loot boxes as gambling. The second is Asian countries, in particular China, South Korea, and Japan, which have taken control of this area, which turned out to be a fairly effective method and helped protect the interests of their own citizens and consumers of gaming content. The third model proposed by scientists is self-regulation of this industry, which can become really effective after some subordination of this sphere to state regulation, since the giants of the gaming industry can take responsibility for changing the rules for microtransactions in favor of consumers either in the presence of significant competition in the market, or under the influence of state coercion (as in the example of Asian countries).

detail.abstract: Arbitration presents a cheap and fast option for resolving health care payment disputes, but it is unclear how individual arbitrators affect resolution outcomes. This paper estimates arbitrator effects on payment determinations made in a clearinghouse for dispute resolution where parties jointly choose an arbitrator to decide their case. Giving disputing parties choice over their arbitrator can be beneficial if parties are better informed about their dispute and the set of arbitrators than a planner, but competition among arbitrators to be chosen may distort their decisions. The No Surprises Act, a 2022 law enacted in the United States, established a centralized platform for disputing health care providers and insurers to select an arbitrator to resolve their disagreement. Among 7 arbitrators, the highest-and lowest-awarding differ by 21% (on a mean of $1,379) in their payment awards to physicians for observably identical cases. This paper finds that the No Surprises Act's arbitration platform established a market for arbitrators; arbitrators compete on payment generosity to physicians, leading to different allocations between physicians and insurers for the same health care visit.

title: Financial Decision Making in the Age of AI
affiliations: Arizona State University (ASU) - W.P. Carey School of Business

detail.title: Financial Decision Making in the Age of AI
detail.abstract: This article gives perspective on the academic literature on personal financial decision making. I explore three main domains of financial choices: savings versus consumption, investment decision making, and choices around debt. In each domain, people behave in ways that deviate from normative prescriptions of financial economics. I explore the main drivers of financial decisions that result in these deviations. The article concludes with a forward-looking perspective of how generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) might reshape the landscape of individual's financial decisions.

title: Inflation Expectations, Investment, and the Mundell-Tobin Financing Channel
affiliations: Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Sloan School of Management and Bank of Italy

detail.title: Inflation Expectations, Investment, and the Mundell-Tobin Financing Channel
detail.abstract: Using a randomized information experiment on Italian firms, we show that the investment response to inflation expectations depends systematically on the horizon of those expectations and on the pledgeability of capital. The tangible investment semi-elasticity with respect to expected inflation nearly doubles as the forecast horizon extends from six months to five years, and is roughly four times larger than the corresponding intangible response. These joint facts are difficult to reconcile with standard valuation or money illusion mechanisms but are consistent with a Mundell-Tobin financing channel in which firms lock in long-term nominal borrowing to fund tangible assets.

title: Creative Ownership in the Age of AI
affiliations: Northwestern University and University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) - Department of Economics

detail.title: Creative Ownership in the Age of AI
detail.abstract: Copyright law focuses on whether a new work is "substantially similar" to an existing one, but generative AI can closely imitate style without copying content, a capability now central to ongoing litigation. We argue that existing definitions of infringement are ill-suited to this setting and propose a new criterion: a generative AI output infringes on an existing work if it could not have been generated without that work in its training corpus. To operationalize this definition, we model generative systems as closure operators mapping a corpus of existing works to an output of new works. AI generated outputs are permissible if they do not infringe on any existing work according to our criterion. Our results characterize structural properties of permissible generation and reveal a sharp asymptotic dichotomy: when the process of organic creations is light-tailed, dependence on individual works eventually vanishes, so that regulation imposes no limits on AI generation; with heavy-tailed creations, regulation can be persistently constraining.

title: Partial Moments as a Unifying Primitive: Distributional Structure, Benchmark-Relative Utility, Adaptive Estimation, and Learned Neural Nonlinearities
affiliations: OVVO Financial Systems

detail.title: Partial Moments as a Unifying Primitive: Distributional Structure, Benchmark-Relative Utility, Adaptive Estimation, and Learned Neural Nonlinearities
detail.abstract: This paper establishes that directional deviation operators of the form ((t-x)_+^r) and ((x-t)_+^r), for integer (r >= 0), constitute a unifying primitive across probability theory, classical moment analysis, expected utility, nonparametric regression, and neural network design. We show that the cumulative distribution function arises as the degree-zero partial moment, and that all central moments admit exact signed decompositions into upper and lower partial moments without approximation. Building on this representation, we embed dual-benchmark utility within the von Neumann–Morgenstern expected utility framework, demonstrating that concavity in gains and convexity in losses emerge from deviation magnification rather than probability weighting. We further prove pointwise and mean-square consistency of a recursive mean-split partition estimator under standard diameter-shrinkage and occupancy conditions, interpreting its partition diameter as a stochastic, data-adaptive bandwidth. Finally, we introduce Partial Moment Activation (PMA), a neural network activation function instantiating the upper partial moment operator with learnable degree (n) and threshold (tau). Empirical results on character-level language modeling and spatial classification demonstrate that trained networks endogenously recover depth-stratified degree progressions consistent with the curvature structure of dual-benchmark utility: sub-linear compression in early layers ($n < 1$) transitioning to super-linear sharpening in late layers (n > 1). A normalized LPM auxiliary loss, derived from the same primitive, yields consistent perplexity improvements across datasets and architectures. We further show that the degree-(n) LPM.ratio family from Section 2 — which generates distorted CDFs over any distribution — provides a theoretical foundation for Partial Moment Attention Functions, a generalization of softmax in which each attention head learns independent curvature and threshold over its score distribution. The results are algebraic where representational and asymptotic where necessary, requiring no density or parametric assumptions. Together, these findings formalize a deviation-based representation framework linking distributional structure, moment identities, benchmark-relative utility, adaptive nonparametric estimation, and learned neural nonlinearities.

title: The House Always Wins: Google's Control of the AdTech Auction
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: The House Always Wins: Google's Control of the AdTech Auction
detail.abstract: This article examines Google's alleged anti-competitive practices in India's programmatic advertising sector through the Alliance of Digital India Foundation's (ADIF) complaint before the Competition Commission of India (CCI) in Case No. 23(1) of 2024. The article analyses Google's systematic abuse of its dominant position across the advertising technology supply chain, focusing on three primary allegations: anti-competitive tying of its Publisher Ad Server with its Ad Exchange, coercive bundling of its Demand Side Platform with AdX access, and exploitation of "Dynamic Allocation" and "Last Look" advantages that disadvantage competitors. This article contextualizes these allegations within comparative regulatory findings, examining parallel decisions by competition authorities worldwide. These international precedents demonstrate consistent global recognition of Google's market manipulation across multiple jurisdictions over seven years, establishing a compelling foundation for similar enforcement action in India and highlighting the urgent need for structural remedies to address Google's systematic abuse of market dominance.

title: Group-Specific Heterogeneity in Short Binary Outcome Panels
affiliations: University of Bonn - Department of Economics

detail.title: Group-Specific Heterogeneity in Short Binary Outcome Panels
detail.abstract: When the number of time periods is small, identification of binary outcome panel data models that allow for heterogeneity is inherently difficult. This paper presents identification and estimation results for such models in the presence of latent group-specific heterogeneity. We assume that each unit belongs to a time-invariant latent group, so the joint distribution of the binary outcomes conditional on the covariates is a finite mixture model. Under mild conditions, the group-specific conditional outcome models are fully nonparametrically identified, with identification being possible with as few as two time periods. We also provide conditions under which group-specific average marginal effects are identified. In addition, we develop a novel semiparametric estimator for the setup of interest and study its asymptotic properties. Simulations indicate that the estimator performs well in finite samples. We illustrate the estimation procedure and how to interpret the latent groups empirically in the context of homeownership in Germany.

detail.abstract: We document persistent racial disparities in U.S. mortgage approval using the near-universe of Home Mortgage Disclosure Act (HMDA) applications, 2020-2024 (42,323,519 applications; 5,567 lending institutions). Black applicants face a 14.95 percentage-point lower approval rate than White applicants; 98.6% of the gap in the estimation sample (raw gap: 14.30 pp) remains unexplained after DiNardo-Fortin-Lemieux (DFL) reweighting on observable characteristics. Within-lender fixed effects indicate that 74.6% of the gap arises within the same institution (mean within-lender penalty: 10.61 pp, p < 0.001). We provide quasi-experimental evidence through two designs. A regression discontinuity at the 80% loan-to-value (LTV) threshold reveals an additional 2.00 pp Black approval penalty (p < 0.001). A difference-indifferences (DiD) design exploiting the 2022 Federal Reserve tightening shows the racial penalty widened by 1.48 pp (p < 0.001); a structural break test confirms 2022 is a discrete shift 2.4 times the prior trend. A triple-difference indicates the two designs operate through distinct channels (p = 0.003). Exact permutation inference shows both the RDD (θ =-1.88 pp) and DiD (δ =-1.01 pp) subsample estimates exceed all 1,000 permuted values (p < 0.001). The threshold effect concentrates in purchase loans (θ =-2.47 pp, p < 0.01) and is absent in refinance loans (n.s.), consistent with the private mortgage insurance (PMI) mechanism. Results are robust to covariate specification and credit-score bounding (lower bound: 9.89 pp, 68.3% of gap).

title: The Digital Offshore: What Jeffrey Epstein Likely Saw in Bitcoin
affiliations: Marquette University

detail.title: The Digital Offshore: What Jeffrey Epstein Likely Saw in Bitcoin
detail.abstract: This article explores Jeffrey Epstein's financial habits, focusing on his longstanding efforts to evade traditional banking oversight and his early interest in emerging financial technologies such as Bitcoin. While there is no evidence linking cryptocurrency to his criminal activity, newly released records and reporting reveal that Epstein studied and invested in technology, seeking ways to minimize reliance on regulated intermediaries. The piece argues that Epstein's attraction to Bitcoin's features, especially its capacity to bypass formal banking structures, parallels the reasons cryptocurrency later became popular in illicit financial networks.

title: Continuous Trading Reveals Expected Returns
affiliations: De Nederlandsche Bank (DNB) and Rabobank International, Netherlands

detail.title: Continuous Trading Reveals Expected Returns
detail.abstract: We show that in models where securities trading is assumed to be continuous, traders can directly observe the drift and volatility of a security using market prices. All uncertainty on these parameter values is therefore eliminated. One implication of this result is that the model of Black and Scholes (1973) cannot be used to determine the price of an option unless one is willing to assume that traders know the expected return on the underlying stock. The belief that Black and Scholes (1973) avoided this assumption, however, was a key contributor to the popularity of their formula.

detail.abstract: For decades, managers in shipping industry have been taught that debt can be a powerful tool to boost returns on equity (ROE). The logic is simple: if a shipping company can mitigate bankruptcy costs, the use of debt will consistently enhance profits for shareholders. But a recent academic study shows that business reality is more complex. Under certain combinations of debt cost and loan maturity, even moderate borrowing can erode, rather than enhance, ROE. Managers should be aware that leverage is not always their friend.

title: Suicide in Working-Age Adults: Determinants, Methods, and Prevention Strategies in Global and Colombian Contexts, a Narrative Review
affiliations: Pontificia Universidad Javeriana, Pontificia Universidad Javeriana, Pontificia Universidad Javeriana and Departamento de Medicina Preventiva y Social, Facultad de Medicina, Pontificia Universidad Javeriana

detail.title: Suicide in Working-Age Adults: Determinants, Methods, and Prevention Strategies in Global and Colombian Contexts, a Narrative Review

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None to declare.
declarations.funderStatement: None.

detail.abstract: Background: Suicide remains a major global public health concern, with marked regional disparities despite declining age-standardized mortality rates worldwide. In Latin America, including Colombia, suicide rates have shown concerning patterns, particularly among economically active populations. Working-age adults are exposed to unique clinical, psychosocial, occupational, and structural stressors that may increase vulnerability to suicidal behavior. Objective: To synthesize global and Colombian evidence on determinants and methods of suicide among working-age adults and to identify evidence-based and culturally sensitive prevention strategies. Methods: This study conducted a narrative literature review using PubMed, Scopus AI, Web of Science AI, and SciELO, complemented by institutional reports from the World Health Organization and Colombian public health sources. Studies published between 2000 and 2025 in English and Spanish were included. Findings were categorized into conceptual domains using an inductive analytical approach. Results: Suicide among working-age adults emerges from the interaction of depressive disorders, substance use, chronic physical illness, psychosocial adversity, and occupational and socioeconomic stressors. In Latin America and Colombia, rural residence and structural inequality shape vulnerability. Hanging is the predominant suicide method globally and regionally, while intoxication predominates in attempts. Evidence supports multilevel prevention strategies that integrate clinical care, workplace-based interventions, community programs, and restriction-of-means policies. Digital interventions show promise but require further evaluation. Conclusions: Suicide in working-age adults represents a complex, multilevel public health issue. Context-sensitive prevention strategies that integrate mental health care, occupational health approaches, and structural policy measures could be essential to reduce suicide mortality in Colombia and similar settings.

detail.abstract: This paper examines labor risk matrices as institutional mechanisms that reshape the interaction between labor law, corporate governance, and economic development. Departing from the traditional view of labor compliance as a defensive and cost-oriented activity, the analysis reframes structured labor risk management systems as informal insurance mechanisms that internalize uncertainty and stabilize firms' expectations. By mapping, quantifying, and anticipating labor-related contingencies, firms reduce transaction costs, mitigate litigation volatility, and allocate resources more efficiently. The paper further argues that mature labor risk governance systems function as economically relevant intangible assets, influencing firm valuation, access to capital, and strategic decision-making, despite their absence from formal balance sheets. From a Law & Economics perspective, labor risk matrices contribute to predictability, contractual efficiency, and institutional stability, particularly in jurisdictions marked by high litigation rates and discretionary enforcement. The study concludes that labor risk governance should be understood not merely as compliance infrastructure, but as a value-generating component of modern economic organization with meaningful implications for sustainable development.

detail.abstract: This study proposes an interdisciplinary framework for managing crisis states during the initial entry of women into the penintentiary system, integrating trauma psychology with prevention economics. Based on 339 days of autoethnographic participant observation, the research identifies the initial intake stage as a critical "psychic risk zone" where acute stress often transitions into costly dissociative states and behavior destabilization. The author proposes the implementation of biologically based express-intervention protocols  (grounding and sensory regulation scripts) designed to maintain cognitive control and prevent psychophysiological decompensation. From an institutional audit perspective, the study demonstrates that early stabilization serves as a crucial risk-management tool. By prevention of escalation crisis into cronic PTSD or social marginalization, these interventions potentially reduce long-term state expenditures related to specialized psychiatric care, lost work capacity and intergenerational social costs. The paper concludes that psychological safety should be redefined as a factor of institutional efficiency and economic rationality.

title: Hurricane Season and Insurer Performance: Third-Quarter Storm Impacts on U.S. Homeowners Loss Ratios, 2013-2024

detail.title: Hurricane Season and Insurer Performance: Third-Quarter Storm Impacts on U.S. Homeowners Loss Ratios, 2013-2024
detail.abstract: This study examines how third-quarter tropical cyclone activity affects loss ratios for U.S. homeowners insurers between 2013 and 2024. Using a firm-state-year panel built from A.M. Best financial data, FEMA/NOAA catastrophe records, and landfall data, we estimate two-way fixed-effects models with robust standard errors clustered at the state level. The models distinguish between storm presence and intensity, split hurricanes from tropical storms, and interact storms with a long-run exposure index, while controlling for state-level unemployment and house-price growth. Results show that third-quarter storm years are associated with higher unconditional loss ratios, but simple storm-occurrence dummies explain very little variation once fixed effects and macro controls are introduced.One-year lag effects are small and generally insignificant. These findings suggest that most storm-related underwriting impacts are realized within the storm year, and that idiosyncratic firm-state factors dominate variation in homeowners loss ratios.

title: Substituting the Future for the Past A Decomposition Analysis Using MarketSim
affiliations: New York University (NYU) - Institute for Policy Integrity and New York University

detail.title: Substituting the Future for the Past A Decomposition Analysis Using MarketSim
detail.abstract: Integrating potential climate action into regulatory analyses is critical for accurately evaluating energy and environmental policies. This paper explores its impact through the federal offshore oil and gas leasing program. Fossil fuel production on federal lands and waters is a significant source of greenhouse gas emissions in the US, yet government models often assume continued reliance on fossil fuels and overlook ongoing climate initiatives, thereby underestimating the climate impacts of leasing policies. Using the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management’s Market Simulation Model, we identify key energy-elasticity parameters driving the net climate effects of offshore leasing. We show theoretically that increased substitutability between fossil fuels and renewables under future climate action could result in more elastic energy demand. Informed by these theoretical predictions and recent literature, we demonstrate that incorporating potential shifts in energy production and consumption patterns into policy baselines significantly increases the projected net climate effects from offshore leasing.

title: The Impact of Energy Price Shocks on US Local Industries: a State-level Analysis
affiliations: Pennsylvania State University and Pennsylvania State University

detail.title: The Impact of Energy Price Shocks on US Local Industries: a State-level Analysis
detail.abstract: Economic activity consumes large amounts of energy, making modern economies especially vulnerable to energy price shocks. Following such a shock, firms adjust by reducing output or energy used per unit of output. Here we use annual panel data for the 50 US States to examine how local industries have adapted to energy price changes since 2000. We estimate a recursive dynamic system that models how energy prices affect output both directly and indirectly through induced capital adjustment and energy intensity. We find that energy price increases reduce local GDP in the short run but also lead to long-term increases in energy efficiency. Output contracts in the short run, but dynamic efficiency gains mitigate these losses: on average, improvements in energy intensity offset between 2% to 5% of the short run GDP decline. We interpret these dynamics as evidence of induced energy-saving technological adjustment, whereby endogenous efficiency adaptation leads to a decoupling of energy consumption from economic growth as energy price rise at the State level.

title: Clean fuel use, Political representation and Forest cover: Evidence from Rural India
affiliations: University of Kalyani and University of Kalyani

detail.title: Clean fuel use, Political representation and Forest cover: Evidence from Rural India
detail.abstract: This paper examines how political representation for marginalized groups affects development outcomes and environmental choices by studying the adoption of clean cooking fuels under India’s Pradhan Mantri Ujjwala Yojana (PMUY). Focusing on political reservations for Scheduled Tribes (STs), we assess how these institutional arrangements influence household fuel use across ecologically diverse regions. Using village-level data from the 2020 Mission Antyodaya Survey and high-resolution forest cover data, we employ a geographic regression discontinuity design (GRD) to compare LPG adoption between Scheduled Areas (administratively designated tribal-majority regions) and non-Scheduled Areas. We find that ST political reservations at the assembly constituency level are associated with a significant reduction in PMUY uptake in Scheduled Areas. To explore variation within SAs, we employ Propensity Score Matching to assess the impact of the Panchayat Extension to Scheduled Areas Act (PESA), which mandates ST representation in local governance. We find that PESA increases LPG adoption in villages located in open forest and scrubland, while it reduces uptake in regions with moderately dense forests. Additionally, our analysis reveals that PESA implementation is linked to forest gains—suggesting that politically empowered ST leaders may promote conservation, inadvertently reinforcing biomass dependence. Our findings highlight a policy trade-off between environmental stewardship and the clean energy transition in ecologically sensitive tribal areas.

title: The Macroeconomics of Hydrogen Sourcing Strategies in a Stock-Flow Consistent Input-Output Model for Germany
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and German Aerospace Center (DLR)

detail.title: The Macroeconomics of Hydrogen Sourcing Strategies in a Stock-Flow Consistent Input-Output Model for Germany
detail.abstract: This paper investigates how hydrogen sourcing strategies shape macroeconomic outcomes in Germany. Using a dynamic stock-flow consistent input-output model with 72 production sectors, we integrate hydrogen-specific investment, technology substitution, and import price shocks into a demand-led macro-financial framework that jointly captures production networks, cost formation, and balance-sheet dynamics.Hydrogen-related investments in production, infrastructure, and downstream technologies raise gross capital formation and stimulate upstream sectors, while the substitution of fossil gas with hydrogen alters sectoral unit costs and propagates through input-output linkages under cost-plus pricing. At the same time, higher investment and changing prices modify debt service, income distribution, and real purchasing power, feeding back into aggregate demand. Through these mechanisms transition generates a pronounced investment cycle that raises employment and output, but aggregate GDP gains remain modest. Under fully domestic production, real GDP increases by up to 0.31\% and employment by 0.45\%, whereas import-oriented pathways exhibit weaker and less persistent employment effects. Consumer prices increase by up to 0.59\%, and partial wage indexation leads to real wage compression and a shift toward profit and interest income. Lower hydrogen prices do not necessarily imply lower inflation, because cheaper hydrogen accelerates adoption, increases its share in intermediate inputs, and thereby amplifies cost pass-through across the input-output network. Hydrogen sourcing therefore emerges as a structural macroeconomic allocation problem, characterised by a quantifiable trade-off between domestic value creation, price stability, and resilience, rather than a pure cost-minimisation choice.

detail.abstract: Coordination failures are commonly attributed to insufficient information, misaligned incentives, or communication breakdown. This framework proposes an alternative account: coordination operates through attractor-class states whose basins are accessible via minimal shared reference primitives (Common-Knowledge Coordination Signals, or CKCS), and which cannot in general be reliably entered through arbitrarily rich but unstructured information or increased coupling alone. This implies that coordination quality and regime membership are distinct phenomena. Systems may possess complete information yet remain unable to enter coordinated states due to basin-access constraints. Conversely, minimal shared reference primitives can enable state transitions that information-rich environments cannot achieve.

title: The Price Impact of Nothing: Rejected Orders as Predictors of Future Returns
affiliations: University of Oxford - Department of Statistics, , University of Oxford - Mathematical Institute and Queen Mary University of London

detail.title: The Price Impact of Nothing: Rejected Orders as Predictors of Future Returns
detail.abstract: The notion of  'price impact' is central to market microstructure. At the level of the mechanical operation of a limit-order-book (LOB) market, order submissions and cancellations are proximately responsible for price changes by removing existing queues and creating new ones, and by altering liquidity without changing the price, which may change subsequently. The term 'price impact of an order' is often used in either of these cases. We probe the extent to which the observable statistical association between orders and price changes is the whole story. We use a uniquely granular dataset, drawn from the blockchain of the cryptocurrency exchange Hyperliquid, which includes rejected maker orders as well as accepted order submissions and cancellations. We focus on 'post-only' maker orders that are rejected as invalid because they would cross the spread; this is a purely mechanical event. These rejected orders, by their nature, cannot affect the LOB in any way and are unobservable to other participants. We show, however, that they are significantly correlated with subsequent price movements. Regression models of the type commonly used to measure price impact yield statistically significant and non-trivial coefficients for measures of rejected order flows. This result is seemingly paradoxical if interpreted directly in terms of the causality of orders: unobserved 'non-orders' appear to have a lasting price impact (in standard usage of the term). The paradox is not real, in that it can be resolved by supposing that rejected and accepted orders alike are responses to a common information set; but it highlights the need for careful use of language in the ascription of causality, as well as the need to revisit perspectives on market operation as new types of data become available.

detail.abstract: Standard equilibrium theory assumes that when incentives align, rational actors will realize optimal outcomes. Yet across domains-nuclear deterrence, migration, climate cooperation, and market coordination-systems frequently remain trapped in suboptimal regimes despite well-understood incentives and complete information. This paper argues that equilibrium optimality is insufficient for equilibrium implementability. I identify a missing variable: conditioning layers-shared, observable coordination infrastructure that collapses second-order uncertainty about mutual intent, timing, and verification. Using Cold War nuclear deterrence as a canonical case, I demonstrate that cooperation became actionable only after explicit coordination mechanisms emerged, despite incentives having been aligned for nearly two decades. I extend this framework to migration dynamics and climate negotiations, showing that action emerges through discontinuous phase transitions when conditioning infrastructure crosses critical density thresholds, not through gradual pressure accumulation. The framework integrates existing work on focal points, common knowledge, and institutions while generating falsifiable predictions about coordination timing, threshold effects, and the relative efficacy of infrastructure interventions versus incentive modifications.

title: Digital Imperialism and Evolutionary Mismatch: A Diagnosis of Modern Capitalism and a Proposal for the "Dancing U.N."

detail.title: Digital Imperialism and Evolutionary Mismatch: A Diagnosis of Modern Capitalism and a Proposal for the "Dancing U.N."
detail.abstract: The Problem: Today, we are living in a new age of "Digital Imperialism." In the 19th century, powerful nations colonized physical land. Today, giant tech companies colonize our minds. By using smartphones, our "attention" has become the newest commodity to be bought and sold. The Theory: This paper explains why this is happening through two lenses: Marxist Theory and Evolutionary Anthropology. Marxism: We are no longer just workers; we are objects of "nerve exploitation." Our focus (attention) is the "Fourth Fictitious Commodity." Evolution: Our bodies are still those of hunter-gatherers. We are designed to explore forests, not scroll through screens. This "Evolutionary Mismatch" is the true cause of modern mental illness, school refusal, and social stress. The Crisis: Civilization has become a "dopamine amplifier." Even war has become a form of addictive entertainment driven by our biological instincts. We are like jockeys on a horse that is running out of control. The Solution: To stop this, we must go beyond "reason" and return to the "body." The author proposes the "Dancing United Nations" model. Before discussing politics, world leaders should dance, use saunas, and share meals to synchronize their nervous systems. To achieve world peace, we must first calm our biological bodies.

title: The "Neutrinos" of the Order Book: Pervasive, Weakly Interacting Order Flow and its Consequences
affiliations: University of Oxford - Department of Statistics, , University of Oxford - Mathematical Institute and Queen Mary University of London

detail.title: The "Neutrinos" of the Order Book: Pervasive, Weakly Interacting Order Flow and its Consequences
detail.abstract:
We consider in detail how liquidity in a limit order book (LOB) is replenished immediately after the spread widens --- the first stage of a price change. To this end, we use a highly granular dataset which we acquire directly from the blockchain of the blockchain-based exchange Hyperliquid. We analyze the entire message flow (approximately 4.5 billion messages over one month) relating to the Bitcoin perpetual contract, which has an average daily turnover of approximately $3 billion.

We reveal the "neutrinos" of the order book: a massive, pervasive, yet weakly interacting flow of post-only limit orders—most of which are mechanically rejected because they would cross the spread—accounting for approximately 67% of all messages sent to the exchange. Such orders, when rejected (which is the vast majority of cases) do not appear in any standard market data feed and are effectively invisible to all traders except the submitter. Nevertheless, they are submitted in vast quantities and almost continuously, by a small group of traders.

We argue that these traders are implementing a strategy to capture favourable queue priority (as part of market-making). They bombard the exchange with orders, most of which are rejected, but a small fraction arrive immediately after a spread-widening event, and secure the desired queue position. We present detailed evidence that the traders are submitting in an extraordinarily accurate directional manner, presumably in response to private and common signals, and we show how the strategy has an embedded risk management which exploits the exchange's own operational controls. We also show that the strategy accounts for a large proportion of "flickering orders" and that it is indeed profitable. Finally, we propose empirical signatures that may help detect whether the strategy is being used in markets where data on rejected orders is not available.

title: The impact of weekly rainfall on water-related diseases in The Gambia: a time-series analysis of health facility data
affiliations: London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine, London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine, University of Turin, London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine - Medical Research Council Unit The Gambia, London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine - Department of Population Health, London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine - Medical Research Council Unit: The Gambia, London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine and London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine

detail.title: The impact of weekly rainfall on water-related diseases in The Gambia: a time-series analysis of health facility data
detail.abstract: In West Africa, anticipated climatic changes may increase the risk of common water-related diseases, however the evidence is limited. We investigated the risk of diarrheal diseases and skin infections associated with rainfall in rural Gambia, using data on clinic visits (2010-2022) linked to meteorological exposures from the ERA5-Land reanalysis dataset. We conducted time-series regression analysis to assess the risks associated with total weekly rainfall (mm) and weeks with heavy rainfall events (daily rainfall >95th percentile) on diarrheal and skin infection visits, adjusted for weekly average maximum temperature (°C), season and long-term trends. Subgroup analyses were undertaken to examine potential effect modification by age, sex and pathogen category. An increase in weekly total rainfall was associated with an increased risk of both health outcomes, but only up to rainfall values of ~30/35mm. Over a 0-3 week lag, 20mm of weekly rainfall (versus 0mm) was associated with an increased relative risk of diarrheal (1.20 RR; 95% CI: 1.01-1.43) and skin visits (1.39 RR; 95% CI: 1.22-1.58). Age modified rainfall-health associations, with patterns differing by outcome. Stronger associations were found in children under-5 for skin infections, while diarrheal risks were higher among patients 5+ years. Rainfall effects were greatest for bacterial skin and diarrheal visits. Heavy rainfall events were not associated with a change in risk for either health outcome. Adjusting for temperature attenuated rainfall effects. These findings show that weather is an important determinant of disease in this population. More investment in climate-resilient water, sanitation and hygiene measures is needed.

title: The Hero and the Scaffold

detail.title: The Hero and the Scaffold
detail.abstract: This essay argues that competence is not an individual attribute but an organizational product. Using the case of René Favaloro-the Argentine cardiac surgeon who pioneered coronary artery bypass grafting at the Cleveland Clinic and returned to found an institution in Buenos Aires-the essay traces how the myth of exceptional individual merit systematically obscures the institutional density required to produce and sustain technical excellence. It examines the mechanisms by which this displacement operates in medicine, academia, and public administration, and concludes with an analysis of how systems that cannot incorporate autonomous institutions of high technical quality are structured to eliminate them.

title: Auditability and Institutional Design in Statutory Disclosure Regimes: Evidence from the EFTA Repository

detail.title: Auditability and Institutional Design in Statutory Disclosure Regimes: Evidence from the EFTA Repository
detail.abstract: The public release of the Epstein Files under the Epstein Files Transparency Act (EFTA) was presented as an unprecedented act of transparency. This study evaluates the disclosure regime not in terms of volume released, but in terms of institutional auditability. Drawing on accountability theory, principal-agent frameworks, and epistemological standards of replicability and traceability, the paper introduces the concept of an auditability threshold: a minimal set of structural conditions required for disclosure to support independent verification. These conditions include corpus enumerability, consolidated inventory export, metadata integrity, searchability, and traceable indexing. Using a stratified sample of documents across the twelve published Data Sets, the study assesses indexability, metadata completeness, redaction density, contextual traceability, and repository-level structural properties. Particular attention is given to the absence of publicly disclosed file counts and consolidated inventory architecture, treated as an independent structural variable rather than a logistical limitation. Comparative analysis with truth commission archives and regulatory data room systems demonstrates that large-scale disclosure can be engineered to satisfy auditability conditions. The deficiencies observed in the EFTA repository therefore reflect architectural design choices rather than unavoidable constraints of scale. The findings indicate that formal compliance with statutory disclosure mandates does not guarantee functional transparency. Where enumerability and navigable structure are absent, transparency produces informational mass without epistemic usability. The paper concludes by proposing minimum design standards for verifiable transparency in future statutory disclosure frameworks.

title: The Identity Gap in Machine-to-Machine Payments: Why Current Infrastructure Cannot Support Autonomous Agent Commerce

detail.title: The Identity Gap in Machine-to-Machine Payments: Why Current Infrastructure Cannot Support Autonomous Agent Commerce
detail.abstract: The autonomous AI agent economy is emerging, but payment infrastructure has not kept pace. We identify a structural gap: fiat payment rails require human identity and authorization that software agents cannot provide, while cryptocurrency rails like Lightning Network lack the organizational identity that commercial API providers require. This "identity gap" prevents legitimate agent commerce from scaling. We analyze the requirements of both sides-agents needing to pay and providers needing accountability-and show why neither fiat nor current crypto solutions satisfy both. The gap represents both a market failure and an infrastructure opportunity.
